consideration. The presumption under Section 118(a) of the said Act 
is rebuttable. The accused neither adduced evidence nor cross-
examined P.W. 1 to rebut the presumption under Section 118(a) of 
the said Act. Therefore I am of the view that the accused issued the 
cheque in favour of the payee-complainant for consideration. The 
prosecution proved the charge against the accused beyond all 
reasonable doubt and the trial Court on proper assessment and 
evaluation of the evidence legally passed the impugned judgment 
and order of conviction. 
Considering the gravity of the offence, I am of the view that 
the ends of justice would be best served if the sentence passed by the 
trial Court is modified as under;  
  The accused Sorower Molla is found guilty of the offence 
under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and he is 
sentenced thereunder to pay a fine of Tk. 11,00,000.  
The complainant-respondent No. 2 is entitled to get the fine 
amount.  
The complainant-respondent No. 2 admitted that he received 
Tk. 5,50,000 from the appellant. Therefore, he is entitled to 
withdraw the remaining fine amount of Tk. 5,50,000 deposited by 
the appellant in the trial Court before filing appeal.  
With the above findings, observation, direction and 
proposition, the appeal is disposed of with a modification of the 
sentence.

order passed by the trial Court and the records. 
On perusal of the records, it appears that the accused Md. 
Shah Alam Dhali issued a cheque on 12.07.2014 in favour of the 
complainant BRAC Bank Limited for payment of Tk. 1,95,036 
(exhibit 3). The said cheque was presented to the BRAC Bank 
Limited, Chandpur Branch on 22.07.2014 but the same was 
dishonoured with a remark ‘insufficient funds’ and the bank issued 
the dishonour slip (exhibit 4). After that, the complainant bank sent 
a notice on 04.08.2014 through registered post with AD to the 
accused which was proved as exhibit 5. P.W. 1 proved the postal 
receipt and AD as exhibits 6 and 7.  
On perusal of the acknowledgement due, it appears that the 
appellant received the notice on 07.08.2014. Despite the notice 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
received by the appellant on 07.08.2014, he did not pay the cheque 
amount. During the trial, the accused was not present and he did not 
cross-examine P.W. 1. Therefore, the evidence of P.W. 1 regarding 
the 
issuance 
of 
the 
cheque 
by 
the 
appellant 
remained 
uncontroverted. I am of the view that the appellant issued the cheque 
(exhibit 3) for payment of Tk. 1,95,036.    
There is a presumption under Section 118(a) of the 
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 that every negotiable instrument 
was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such 
instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or 
transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for 
consideration. The presumption under Section 118(a) of the said Act 
is rebuttable. The accused neither adduced evidence nor cross-
examined P.W. 1 to rebut the presumption under Section 118(a) of 
the said Act. Therefore I am of the view that the accused issued the 
cheque in favour of the payee-complainant for consideration. The 
cheque was dishonoured and after service of notice in writing under 
Section 138(1)(b) of the said Act, the accused did not pay the 
cheque amount. Thereby the accused committed an offence under 
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and the 
complainant filed the case following all procedures provided in 
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The 
prosecution proved the charge against the accused beyond all 
reasonable doubt and the trial Court on proper assessment and 
evaluation of the evidence legally passed the impugned judgment 
and order. 
In view of the above evidence, findings, observation and 
proposition, I am of the view that the prosecution proved the charge 
against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt and the trial Court 
on proper assessment and evaluation of the evidence legally 
convicted the accused.  

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
On perusal of the judgment passed by the trial Court, it 
appears that the trial Court awarded a sentence of rigorous 
imprisonment against the accused. No provision is made in Section 
138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 to award rigorous 
imprisonment. The trial Court is only empowered to award a simple 
sentence against the accused provided that the prosecution proved 
the charge against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt.  
Considering the gravity of the offence, I am of the view that 
the ends of justice would be best served if the impugned sentence 
passed by the trial Court is modified as under;  
 The accused Md. Shah Alam Dhali is found guilty of the 
offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 
and he is sentenced to suffer imprisonment for 2(two) months and a 
fine of Tk. 1,95,036. 
The accused Md. Shah Alam Dhali is directed to surrender 
forthwith and pay the remaining 50% of the cheque amount within 
30(thirty) days from the date failing which the trial Court is directed 
to do the needful.   
In the result, the appeal is disposed of. 
Send down the lower Court’s records at once.
input_summary: The appellant had taken a loan from a bank and, on failing to repay in time, issued a cheque for the outstanding amount, which the bank presented and which came back unpaid for insufficient funds. The bank served a notice by registered post, which the appellant received, but he paid nothing, and a complaint followed. The bank's officer proved the cheque, the dishonour slip, the notice, the postal receipt and the acknowledgement; the appellant did not cross-examine him, adduced no evidence and was absent. He was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for a year and a fine, and he challenged that in appeal.
explanation: The court found that the bank had complied with every requirement of the statutory provision: the cheque was proved, dishonour for insufficient funds was established, notice was received and the amount remained unpaid, and the presumption that the instrument was drawn for consideration had not been rebutted, the appellant having neither led evidence nor tested the prosecution witness. The conviction was accordingly sustained. The court, however, noticed an error in the sentence, in that no power exists under that provision to award rigorous imprisonment, the court being competent only to impose a simple sentence. The punishment was therefore reduced to a short simple term together with the fine, with a direction to pay the balance.

explanation: The court noted that the offence is not compoundable and that the conviction could not be undone merely because the parties had settled, but it referred to a decision of the apex court in which, upon a compromise and payment of half the cheque amount in cash with the rest deposited, the sentence was reduced to the period already undergone and the complainant was permitted to withdraw the money. This is an application for withdrawal of Title Suit No. 115 of 
2003 with permission to institute a fresh suit in respect of the self-
same subject matter. 
It is stated in the instant application that the present petitioner 
as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 115 of 2003 in the Court of Senior 
Assistant Judge, Sreenagar, Munshigonj for declaration of title in the 
suit land and for partition of the same. The suit was dismissed on 
contest on 11.11.2004 (decree signed on 25.11.2004). Title Appeal 
No. 09 of 2005 was dismissed on contest by the learned District 

<<PAGE 2>>
: 2 : 
 
Judge, Munshigonj on 24.07.2005. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff filed 
the instant revisional application and obtained the Rule. 
It is further stated in the instant application that it is stated in 
the plaint that the suit land is recorded in R.S. Khatian No. 1 as khas 
land. The learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner 
submits that instead of filing suit for declaration of title and partition, 
the plaintiff ought to have filed suit for declaration of title with a 
prayer for correction of the relevant R.S. Khatian. The learned 
Advocate further submits that the plaintiff ought to have tendered in 
evidence rent receipt No. A 952230 dated 02.08.1961, rent receipt No. 
F 877806 dated 14.05.1963 and rent receipt No. D 475216 dated 
14.04.1967 in support of his case. Those rent receipts have been 
annexed to the instant application and marked as Annexure-A, B and 
C respectively. The learned Advocate further submits that in the 
attending facts and circumstances, if the plaintiff’s application is not 
allowed, he shall be highly prejudiced and shall suffer irreparable loss 
and injury. In support of the submission, the learned Advocate refers 
to the cases reported in 25 DLR 485 and 54 DLR 416. 
I have heard the learned Advocate of the plaintiff-applicant and 
the learned Assistant Attorney General. Be it mentioned that various 
concerned offices of the government are defendants in the case. 
It is settled principle of law that there is no legal bar in granting 
an application for withdrawal of a suit with liberty to file a suit afresh 

<<PAGE 3>>
: 3 : 
 
on the self-same matter even at a revisional stage provided the other 
requirements of the law are complied with. 
On perusal of the revisional application, judgments passed by 
the Courts below and other materials on record, it appears that the suit 
in its present form and manner i.e. suit for declaration of title and 
partition is bound to fail. In that view of the matter, I find substance in 
the application. 
Accordingly, the instant application is allowed. The plaintiff is 
permitted to withdraw Title Suit No. 115 of 2003 with liberty to 
institute a fresh suit in respect of the subject matter of the suit if it is 
not otherwise barred by limitation.

respect of possession of the suit land is recalled and vacated.

Rule was issued on an application under section 115(1) of 
the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite party No. 1 
to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 
28.07.1986 passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Pirojpur in Title 
Appeal No. 172 of 1983 reversing those of dated 21.03.1983 
passed by the Munsif, Second Court, Pirojpur in Title Suit No. 76 
of 1981, dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or such 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and 
proper. 
The present opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit 
No. 76 of 1981 in the Second Court of Munsif, Pirojpur for a  
declaration that the order dated 24.12.1979 passed in V.P. Case 
No. 250 of 1979(N) is illegal, void, in-effective, without 
jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The case of the 
plaintiff as stated in the plaint briefly are that the suit property was 
originally belonged to the C.S. recorded tenant Gonga Charan 
Roy,  Provat Charan Roy, Shib Das Roy and Kedarnath Roy in 
equal share. Kedarnath died leaving behind wife Birajmohini, who 
got life interest in Kedarnath’s left 4(four) anas share. Thereafter, 
Birajmohini died leaving behind her husband’s brother, Shib Das 
Roy. On the death of Shib Das Roy, the said 8 (eight) anas share 
was devolved upon Gonga Charan Roy and Provat Charan Roy 
and accordingly, Gonga Charan Roy and Provat Charan Roy 
acquired 8(eight) anas share each in the suit land. The further case 
of the plaintiff is that the suit land was put into auction for arrears 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
of rent by the Deputy Commissioner of Bakergonj in pursuant to 
Certificate Case No. 1274(N) of 1962-63 and the notices were 
duly served thereafter the plaintiff in the said auction purchased 
the suit property which was duly confirmed on 20.03.1964 and 
boynama was issued on 31.01.1966; the plaintiff was inducted 
into the possession on 11.10.1966 through Court. The plaintiff has 
been possessing the suit land on payment of rent to the 
Government. The defendant No. 1 declared the suit land as vested 
property without holding any proper enquiry and it has been 
enlisted as vested property in V.P. Case No. 250 of 1979 vide 
order dated 24.12.1979. Hence the suit. 
Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing written 
statement denying all the material averments made in the plaint 
contending, inter-alia that the recorded tenants Shib Das Roy and 
others left for India in the year 1960 and started living 
permanently therein and as such, the property has been enlisted as 
enemy property and thereafter vested property. The plaintiff in 
order to grab the property fraudulently created an ante-dated 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
certified copy of Certificate Case No. 1274 of 1962-63; the suit 
property was never put in auction for arrears of rent in the said 
certificate case. So the story of purchasing the suit land in 
pursuant to a certificate case was plotted only to grab the property. 
The plaintiff has no possession over the suit land and property has 
been legally declared as vested. The plaintiff has no cause of 
auction to bring the suit and the suit is barred under section 42 of 
the Specific Relief Act as it is not maintainable in its present form.  
On the basis of the pleadings of both the parties, the 
following issues have been framed for adjudication of the suit: 
(i) 
Whether the suit is maintainable in its present 
form? 
(ii) 
Whether the suit is barred under section 42 of 
Specific Relief Act? 
(iii) Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties? 
(iv) 
Whether the plaintiff has any right title interest 
and possession in the suit land? 
(v) 
Whether the order passed in V.P Case No. 250 
of 1979 is illegal, null, void, without 
jurisdiction and binding upon the plaintiff? 
(vi) 
Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get the 
reliefs as prayed for?  

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
Learned Munsif after discussions of all the issues and 
dealing with the evidences and relevant laws dismissed the suit on 
contest by his judgment and decree dated 21.03.1983. 
Having been aggrieved by the said judgment of learned 
Munsif, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 172 of 1983 
before the District Judge, Pirojpur. On transfer the said appeal was 
heard by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Pirojpur and by his judgment 
and decree dated 28.07.1986 allowed the appeal reversed the 
judgment and decree dated 21.03.1983 passed by the Munsif, 
Second Court, Pirojpur in Title Suit No. 76 of 1981 and thereby 
decreed the suit. 
On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid 
judgment and decree of the Sub-ordinate Judge, Pirojpur dated 
28.07.1986 the defendant No. 1 filed this revisional application 
and obtained the Rule in the year 1987.  
Ms. Rashida Alim Oeeshi, learned Deputy Attorney 
General appearing with Mr. Md. Habibur Rahman Sarker, learned 

<<PAGE 6>>
6 
 
Assistant Attorney General for the petitioner and submits that the 
trial Court upon consideration of the pleadings of both the parties 
framed proper issues of law as well as facts. The issue No. 2 was, 
whether the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief 
Act, 1877 (In short the SR Act) or not and after considering the 
relevant provision of section 42 of the SR Act held that the suit is 
barred under section 42. It was also found by the trial Court that 
the original copy of the alleged ‘Sale Certificate’ has not been 
produced by the plaintiff to prove his case or the plaintiff did not 
take any initiative to call for the record to prove the said certificate 
case. It is also found that though the plaintiff claimed that Gonga 
Charan and Provat Charan Roy died within the country, but in his 
cross-examination, P.W. 1 admitted that he cannot say the exact 
date of death of the original recorded owners. He also disclosed in 
the cross that he has no knowledge about the auction which was 
held for how many years arrears rent and he could not submit any 
paper to show that the notices under section 7 of the Public 
Demand Recovery Act, 1913 was duly served upon the Gonga 

<<PAGE 7>>
7 
 
Charan and Provat Charan. And in view of aforesaid findings of 
fact learned Munsif dismissed the suit. She continues to submit 
that but the Court of appeal below without controverting the 
aforesaid positive and specific findings of fact of the trial Court, 
illegally reversed the judgment and decree upon shifting the onus 
upon the defendants to disprove the plaintiff’s case and thereby 
committed an error of law in the decision occasioning failure of 
justice. She further submits that under 42 of the Specific Relief 
Act, the plaintiff is not entitled to a simple declaration that the 
order dated 24.12.1979 passed in V.P. Case No. 250 of 1979 is 
null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff without first 
establishing his title or legal status over the suit land. Thus, the 
case of the plaintiff is hopelessly barred by section 42 of the 
Specific Relief Act.  
In support of her submission, learned D.A.G cited the case 
of Ratan Chandra Dey and others Vs. Jinnator Nahar and others 
reported in 61 DLR(AD) 116 and the case of KM Zahirul Haque 
Vs. Shahida Khanam and others reported in 12 BLC(AD) 65. 

<<PAGE 8>>
8 
 
Although, the Rule was issued on 05.02.1987 but no one on 
behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party appeared before this Court to 
contest the Rule.  
Heard learned Deputy Attorney General for the petitioner, 
perused the revisional application; having gone through the Lower 
Courts’ Record, the provision of law and cited judgments.  
From the record, it appears that the trial Court came to a 
positive finding that the fact of Certificate Case No. 1274 of 1962-
63 having not been proved by adducing adequate evidence and the 
plaintiff in his cross examination admitted that he had nothing to 
show that the notices under section 7 of the Public Demand 
Recovery Act was duly served and the trial Court also found that 
the plaintiff failed to produce the original copy of the sale 
certificate relates to Certificate Case No. 1274 of 1962-63, the 
basic document of his title and the plaintiff’s witnesses failed to 
support the date and time of delivery of possession and on the 
basis of the aforesaid findings learned Munsif of the trial Court 

<<PAGE 9>>
9 
 
came to the positive conclusion that the auction purchase in 
pursuant to the Certificate Case No. 1274 of 1962-63 having not 
been proved. The trial Court further found that the suit is barred 
under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. 
For better understanding, let us examine the provision of 
section 42, the said provision is reproduced herein below: 
“42. Discretion of Court as to declaration of 
status or right- Any person entitled to any legal 
character, or to any right as to any property, may 
institute a suit against any person denying, or 
interested to deny, his title to such character or right, 
and the Court may in its discretion make therein a 
declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff 
need not in such suit ask for any further relief: 
Bar to such declaration-Provided that no 
Court shall make any such declaration where the 
plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere 
declaration of title, omits to do so. 
Explanation………………………………………
……………………………………………………………” 
 
From the aforesaid provision, it appears that any person 
entitled to any legal character or to any right as to any property 
may institute a suit against any person denying and or interested to 

<<PAGE 10>>
10 
 
deny his title or right to the said property and the Court may in its 
discretion by its verdict made a declaration that the plaintiff is 
entitled to the title or right to such property. In such proceedings, a 
person must establish that at the time of institution of the suit in 
declaratory form he had any legal character or status relates to the 
said suit property. No suit is maintainable under section 42 of the 
Specific Relief Act, unless the plaintiff is entitled to some legal 
character or to some legal right attached to the property and he is 
to sought for and thereby establish that he is entitled to such right. 
Without framing proper suit with proper prayer, the instant suit as 
has been filed by the plaintiff is hit by the provision of section 42 
of the Specific Relief Act. In this regard reliance can be made on 
the judgment of Ratan Chandra Das and others Vs. Jinnator Nahar 
and others reported in 61 DLR(AD) 116 and the case of 
Sheoparsan Singh and Others Vs. Ramnandan Prashad Narayan 
Singh and Others reported in AIR (1916) (PC) 78. 
The Court of appeal below without controverting the 
specific finding of fact of learned Munsif within the stipulation of 

<<PAGE 11>>
11 
 
Order XLI, rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure came to a 
wrong decision reversing those of learned Munsif occasioning 
failure of justice, wrongly shifting the onus upon the defendants to 
prove or disprove the case of the plaintiff.  
In the premise above, this Court do find merit in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order 
as to cost. 
The judgment and decree dated 28.07.1986 passed by the 
Sub-ordinate Judge, Pirojpur in Title Appeal No. 172 of 1983 is 
hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 21.03.1983 
passed by the Munsif, Second Court, Pirojpur in Title Suit No. 76 
of 1981 is hereby restored. 
Send down the Lower Courts’ Record. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once.

The plaintiff had sued for a declaration that an order enlisting the suit property as vested property in a proceeding of the late nineteen seventies was illegal, void and without jurisdiction, pleading purchase of the property at a rent auction long ago with confirmation, certificate and delivery of possession through court, and payment of rent since. The authorities asserted that the recorded tenants had left for India, that the property had therefore been correctly enlisted, and that the alleged auction purchase was a fabrication.
explanation: The court found that the trial court had recorded positive findings that the certificate case had not been proved by adequate evidence, that the plaintiff had conceded in cross-examination that he had nothing to show service of notice under section 7 of the Public Demand Recovery Act, 1913, and that the original sale certificate, the basic document of title, had not been produced, nor delivery of possession supported by his witnesses. The appellate court had reversed those findings without displacing them, shifting the onus onto the defendants. The court further held that a bare declaration that the enlisting order was void was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, unless title was first established. The rule succeeded.

the case in hand, the plaintiff miserably failed to establish that

declaration as sought for. Thus, the suit is hit by section 42 of 
the Specific Relief Act, 1877.  
From the record, it further appears that the plaintiff- 
petitioner challenged the tender notice purportedly floated by 
the defendant No. 1, Pourashava for leasing out the market for 
the year 1985, the tenure of aforesaid tender or lease in question 
was ended in the year 1986. Thus, the suit lost its cause of 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
action long before 38(thirty eight) years, which makes the Rule 
infructuous.  
In the premise above, this Court do not find any merit in 
the Rule.  
Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as 
to cost. 
Send down the Lower Courts’ Record. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Obaidul Hasan/B.O.
input_summary: The petitioner as plaintiff had sued the municipal authority for a declaration that an item in its notice inviting tenders for leasing out a shrimp market at a terminal ghat was illegal, void and without jurisdiction, and for an injunction restraining the authority from realising any tax or toll on account of the shrimp business there. He pleaded that he and other traders had taken lease of government khas land nearby, built houses and run businesses. The authority denied the claim, contending that the suit was not maintainable for want of standing. The trial court decided the suit in the plaintiff's favour, but the appellate court reversed that decision.
explanation: The court noted that neither side appeared, the revision being some thirty-six years old, and took it up on merit. It found that the appellate court had recorded that the plaintiff failed to prove his standing, having produced no paper to show that he had taken settlement of khas land, and that no other trader had furnished any document to support him. It further found the place to be a market within municipal limits which the authority was empowered to lease out in open tender, and held the declaratory suit hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, no right or legal character having been established. The lease term having expired, the cause of action had long perished.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH

The instant civil revision is directed against the order dated 
02.05.2016 passed by the Special District Judge, Barishal in Title 
Appeal No. 06 of 2010 rejecting the application filed by the appellants 
under Order 41 rule 27 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure (CPC) and also rejecting the application for recalling DW-
1. This Court, on 23.10.2016, issued a Rule.  
 
Defendant-appellants are the petitioners. Title Suit No. 87 of 
2003, in which the petitioners and others were defendants, was heard 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
and disposed of analogously with Title Suit No. 82 of 2003 by the 
Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Barishal on 12.02.2009. Title Suit No. 
87 of 2003 was decreed and Title Suit No. 82 of 2003 was dismissed. 
Challenging the decree passed in Title Suit No. 87 of 2003, the 
present petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 67 of 2009, which was 
subsequently renumbered as Title Appeal No. 06 of 2010. 
 
Today, when the matter was taken up for judgment, the learned 
Advocate appearing for the petitioners filed a supplementary affidavit 
annexing the plaint, written statement, judgment and decree passed by 
the trial Court in Title Suit No. 87 of 2003. 
 
During pendency of the title appeal, the appellant-petitioners 
filed an application on 15.04.2014 before the appellate Court below 
for recalling DW-1. The relevant portion of the said application is 
reproduced below:  
DW-1 
Re call
DW-1 
Re call

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
DW-1 
Re call
 
Thereafter, the defendant-appellants on 12.11.2015 filed 
another application before the appellate Court on the same subject 
matter i.e. recalling DW-1 and for permission to produce additional 
evidence. The relevant portion of the said application is quoted below: 
DW-1 
Re call
DW-1 
Re call
 
The appellate Court below rejected both the applications 
observing, inter alia:  
SUBSTANTIAL CAUSE 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
 
I have heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused 
the materials on record. 
 
Mahmudul Islam and Probir Neogi in ‘The Law of Civil 
Procedure’, 2nd ed., vol. 2, at page 1880 observed, “In allowing 
additional evidence three conditions must be fulfilled: (i) it must be 
shown that the evidence could not have been obtained with reasonable 
diligence for use at the trial (25 DLR 108), (ii) the evidence must have 
been such that, if given, it would probably have an important 
influence, though not decisive, on the result of the case (AIR 1931 PC 
143, AIR 1957 Nag 15), and (iii) the evidence must be apparently 
credible although it need not be incontrovertible. In the absence of 
satisfactory reason for non-production of the evidence in the trial 
Court, additional evidence should not be admitted in appeal (AIR 
1915 PC 78).” 
 
In the cases reported in 50 CWN 2(PC), AIR 1957 SC 912 and 
25 DLR 108 it is held that a party shall not be allowed to put in 
additional evidence when the party had ample opportunity to produce 
and prove it in the trial Court. It is held in 8 BLT (AD) 1 that the 
appellate Court should not allow additional evidence without 
sufficient explanation for not filing it at the trial stage.  
In the case in hand, the defendant-appellants did not state in 
their applications the reasons for non-producing the evidence at the 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
trial. They did not offer any explanation whatsoever for not filing the 
additional evidence at the trial stage. There is no statement to that 
effect in the applications filed by the defendant-appellants before the 
appellate Court. This being the position, the Rule fails. 
 
In the result, the Rule is discharged. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Arif, ABO
input_summary: The defendants in a title suit, whose suit was heard together with another and decided against them, carried the matter in appeal and then sought through this revision to undo an order of the appellate court turning down two applications, one for recalling a defence witness and another for permission to adduce additional evidence. They sought to produce the plaint, written statement, judgment and decree of the trial court, and at the hearing furnished a supplementary affidavit annexing those papers. The appellate court had declined the applications, observing that the conditions for receiving additional evidence at the appellate stage were not satisfied.
explanation: The court referred to the conditions settled in the textbooks and in reported decisions for admitting additional evidence at the appellate stage: that the evidence could not have been obtained with reasonable diligence for use at the trial, that it would probably have an important, though not decisive, influence on the result, and that it must be apparently credible; and that additional evidence should not be received where the party had ample opportunity to produce it in the trial court. Applying those tests, the court found that the applications contained no explanation at all for the failure to produce the material at the trial stage. The rule therefore failed.

The present petitioners as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 30 of 
1992 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Golapganj, Sylhet 
impleading (a) Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet, 
(b) the then Thana Nirbahi Officer, Golapganj, Sylhet, and (c) 
Assistant Commissioner (Land), Golapganj, Sylhet as principal 
defendants. Sree Madhusudhan Kabyatirta, Principal, Sreehatta 
Sangskrit College, Sylhet was the pro-forma defendant. Present 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
opposite party No. 1 Sree Sree Radha Muhan Jew Deity was added as 
defendant No. 5, who filed an application before the Court below 
under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) for 
rejection of the plaint on the grounds stated therein. The application 
was opposed by the plaintiffs by filing written objection. The learned 
Assistant Judge, vide judgment and order dated 09.02.1993 allowed 
the application and rejected the plaint. The plaintiffs preferred Title 
Appeal No. 70 of 1993. The learned District Judge, Sylhet, vide 
judgment and order dated 30.04.1995 dismissed the appeal. 
Thereafter, the plaintiffs preferred the instant civil revision and 
obtained Rule.  
None appeared for the plaintiff-petitioners when the Rule was 
taken up for hearing. The added defendant No. 5 (opposite party No. 1 
herein) has entered appearance in the Rule.  
The plaintiffs filed the title suit praying for a declaration that 
they are entitled to perform sheba puja to the deity established at Sree 
Sree Radha Muhan Jew Akhra situated in the scheduled land 
measuring 2.28 acres. The plaintiffs further prayed for a declaration 
that the notice issued under memo No. SA/3316(6) dated 03.10.1992 
by the defendant No. 1 Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), 
Sylhet is illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiffs. 
The plaintiffs also prayed for a permanent injunction to restrain 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
defendants from evicting them from the suit land and to prevent them 
from interfering with the performance of the puja. 
It is stated in the plaint that the plaintiffs’ predecessor late 
pujari Profulla Kumar Bhattacharya was appointed as shebait of the 
Akhra on 30.08.1957 and since then he had performed the puja in the 
Akhra till his death in 1990. After his death, the plaintiffs being the 
legal heirs of late shebait have been performing the puja. It is further 
stated that the land in which the Akhra situates is also used as place of 
residence of the plaintiffs. The pro-forma defendant No. 4 Principal, 
Sreehatta Sangskrit College, Sylhet granted written permission to the 
plaintiff No. 1 to perform the puja in the said Akhra on 25.10.1990. It 
is further stated that the defendant Nos. 1-3 appointed a managing 
committee to run the Akhra and on 03.10.1992 the defendant No. 1 
issued the eviction notice directing the plaintiffs to vacate the land, 
failing which they would be evicted.  
The trial Court rejected the plaint on the ground that the 
eviction notice dated 03.10.1992 was issued under Seciton 5(1) of the 
Government and Local Authority Lands and Buildings (Recovery of 
Possession), Ordinance, 1970 and no illegality was committed in 
issuance of the said notice. The appellate Court below affirmed the 
judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge holding that the 
plaintiffs have no legal character to file the suit in that they claimed to 
perform the puja as legal heirs of the late shebait, but right of 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
shebaitship relating to any deity cannot be acquired by inheritance and 
mere living in the lands belonging to deity does give rise to any legal 
character. 
I have gone through the materials on record and considered the 
submissions of the learned Senior Advocate Mr. Tabarak Hossain 
appearing for the opposite party No. 1.  
It appears from the eviction notice dated 03.10.1992, which is 
submitted by the plaintiffs by way of firisty in the Court below and 
lying with the records, that by the said notice the plaintiffs were 
directed to vacate the property within 07 days, failing which they 
would be evicted in accordance with law on the ground that they are 
unauthorised occupants of the land in which the Akhra situates. It is 
further stated in the notice that the T.N.O., Golapganj (defendant No. 
2) had conducted an enquiry and submitted a report dated 08.09.1992 
in Eviction Case No. 2/92 stating that the plaintiffs are unauthorised 
occupants of the property. The T.N.O. made recommendation to evict 
the plaintiffs.  
The eviction notice does not refer to Section 5 of the Ordinance, 
1970. However, the language used in the notice clearly denotes that 
the same was issued under Section 5. The learned Assistant Judge 
rightly held that the notice was issued in exercise of power vested 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
upon the Deputy Commissioner by Section 5 of the Ordinance, 1970. 
Section 5 is quoted below: 
“5. (1) If the Deputy Commissioner, on his own motion or on 
the complaint of or upon information received from anybody or 
a Local Authority, is satisfied after making such inquiry as he 
thinks fit, that a person is an unauthorised occupant, he may 
issue, in the prescribed manner, a notice directing such person 
to vacate the land, building or part thereof in his occupation 
within a period of thirty days from the date of service of the 
notice.  
Provided that the Deputy Commissioner may, where he is 
satisfied that thirty days' notice will not be in public interest, 
reduce the period of such notice to not less than seven days. 
  (2) If the person, against whom an order under sub-section 
(1) has been made, refuses or fails to vacate the land, building 
or part thereof in his occupation within the time fixed, then, 
notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the 
time being in force, it shall be lawful for the Deputy 
Commissioner to enter upon such land, building or part thereof 
and recover khas possession of the same by evicting such 
person and by demolishing and removing structures, if any, 
erected or built by that person.” 
Mr. Tabarak Hossain refers to Sections 10 and 11 of the 
Ordinance, 1970 and submits that the notice dated 03.10.1992 is 
appealable to the Divisional Commissioner under Section 10 and that 
under Section 11 there is a clear bar on civil Court to grant a 

<<PAGE 6>>
6 
 
temporary or ad-interim injunction. Sections 10 and 11 are quoted 
below: 
“10. Any person aggrieved by an order made under section 3 
or section 4 or section 5 or section 9 may prefer an appeal to the 
Commissioner of the Division within thirty days of the service 
of notice and the decision of the Commissioner on such an 
appeal shall be final. 
11. No civil Court shall pass an order in any suit or 
proceeding granting a temporary or ad interim injunction 
restraining the Deputy Commissioner from taking possession of 
any land, building or part thereof under this Ordinance nor shall 
call in question any assessment of compensation made under 
this Ordinance.” 
In view of the provisions contained in Section 10 that the order 
made under Section 5 to vacate the property is appealable to the 
Divisional Commissioner, the instant suit is barred by law. It is 
categorically stated in the plaint that a new managing committee has 
been appointed for the Akhra but no relief has been sought against the 
said newly appointed managing committee. Therefore, the suit is not 
maintainable in its present form and manner. Therefore, the Rule fails. 
In the result, the Rule is discharged.

Arif, ABO

explanation: The court observed that the trial court had allotted the larger area on the basis of a particular measurement of the schedules, while the appellate court, after re-examining the several title deeds produced and taking note of earlier litigation between the parties, including an earlier direction of this court that the shares be reallocated, found the plaintiffs entitled to a much smaller area as delineated in those schedules. The plaintiffs had sued for a declaration that the enlisting of a large tract as vested and non-resident property and its leasing out to the defendants in a proceeding of the mid-seventies was illegal and not binding, and for a perpetual injunction. explanation: The court noted that a portion of the disputed land had in the meantime been published in the gazette under the Arpito Sampatti Prottarpon Ain, 2012, and held that the proceeding stood abated as to that portion under section 28Ka of that Act. concern of defendant no. 2 and the defendant no. 3 is brother of

However, upon hearing the parties, the learned Joint District

input_summary: The petitioner, a manufacturer and supplier, sued its purchaser and a state-owned enterprise for a substantial sum said to be due for goods delivered, and applied for attachment before judgment of the amount payable by the enterprise to its purchaser, asserting that the purchasers had no other assets. The plaint set out the value of the goods supplied, the part paid and the balance, and identified the sum receivable by the purchaser from the enterprise, with the schedule describing the bill. The trial court turned down the application, holding that the bill was vague and had not been described in the plaint. No one appeared for any of the opposite parties.
explanation: The court found on examination of the record that the plaint had categorically stated the value of the goods supplied, the amount paid and the outstanding balance, and that it identified in clear terms the sum receivable by the purchaser from the enterprise, supported by a letter brought on record and reflected in the schedule to the application. The trial court's premise that the plaint lacked any description was therefore incorrect. The court further noted that two cheques issued by the purchasers had been dishonoured, showing conduct that was not fair, that the claim appeared genuine and that the bill sought to be attached was the only identifiable asset. The order was overturned and attachment directed.

CIVIL REVISION NO.5397 OF 2023

    .…..The plaintiff-opposite parties.

........ For the opposite parties. 
 
 
The 28th, November,2024. 
 
By this Rule, the opposite parties were called upon 
to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and 
order dated 24.05.2023 passed by the learned Additional 
District Judge, 2nd Court, Munshiganj in Title Appeal 
No.140 of 2013, allowing the application under Order VI 
Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of 
plaint.  
Facts leading to this Rule are that the opposite 
parties 1-22 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit 13 of 2011 
before the Senior Assistant Judge, Tongibari, Munshiganj, 
for declaration of title. 
Defendants 1-8 contested the suit by filing a joint 
written statement.  
The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Tongibari, 
Munshiganj, framed necessary issues during the trial. 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Subsequently,  the learned Senior Assistant Judge, 
Tongibari, Munshiganj, dismissed the suit by judgment 
and decree dated 28.03.2013. 
Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal 
No.140 of 2013 before the District Judge, Munshiganj, 
and on transfer, the appeal is pending for disposal before 
the Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Munshiganj. 
During the pendency of the appeal, the plaintiff 
opposite parties 1-22 applied for amendment of plaint 
Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Upon 
hearing the application, the learned Additional District 
Judge, 2nd Court, Munshiganj, by the judgment and order 
dated 24.05.2023, allowed the application to amend the 
plaint. 
Being 
aggrieved, 
the 
defendant-respondent 
as 
petitioners moved this revision before this Court and 
obtained the instant Rule and an order of stay.  
Mr. Md. Abul Kasem, the learned Counsel appearing 
on behalf of the petitioners, submits that the appellate 
Court below committed an error of law resulting in an 
error in the decision, occasioning failure of justice in not 
considered that the applicant applied to an amendment of 
the plaint under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure after judgment and decree because, after 
commencement of trial, there is no scope to allow the 
same unless the Court is satisfied that despite due 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
diligence, the party could not have raised the matter 
before the commencement of trial, moreover the above 
amendment of the plaint changed the nature and 
character of the original suit and as such the impugned 
order of the appellant court is liable to be set aside.  
Mr. 
A.K.M. 
Shamshad, 
the 
learned 
Counsel 
appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, submits that 
as per Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the 
Court has ample power to amend the application at any 
stage of the suit so the appellate Court justifiedly allowed 
the amendment application.  
I have anxiously considered the submission of the 
learned advocate for both parties pursued the impugned 
judgment and order,  amendment application, and the 
other materials on record. It appears that the appellate 
Court below saying that there is no chance of changing 
the nature and character of the suit. So, the application 
for amendment under Order VI Rule 17 is allowed.  
Notably, the law relating to the amendment of  a 
plaint is envisaged in Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure which runs as follows: 
“The court may at any stage of the proceeding 
allow either party to alter or amend his 
pleadings in such manner and on such terms 
as may be just, and all such amendments shall 
be made as may be necessary for the purpose 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
of 
determining 
the 
real 
questions 
in 
controversy between the parties.”  
   It reveals that if any material facts and necessary 
particulars are omitted during the drafting of a plaint, 
such particulars can be added to the pleadings at any 
stage of the proceedings; there should be some foundation 
and basis for such amendment. All amendments that may 
be necessary for determining the real question in 
controversy between the parties may be allowed, provided 
it does not cause injustice or prejudice to the other side. 
Ultimately, courts exist for the purpose of doing justice 
between the parties and not for punishing them, and they 
are empowered to grant amendments in the more 
significant interest of doing complete justice to the parties. 
Provisions for the amendment of pleadings are intended to 
promote the ends of justice and not defeat them. 
It is a well-established principle that the object of 
courts is to decide the rights of the parties and not to 
punish them for mistakes they make in the conduct of 
their cases by deciding otherwise than in accordance with 
their rights. If the error or mistake is not fraudulent or is 
not intended to overreach, the Court ought to correct it if 
it cannot do injustice to the other side. Courts do not exist 
for the sake of discipline but to decide matters in 
controversy. I do not regard such an amendment as a 
matter of favor or grace. It seems that the amendment will 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
help determine the fundamental controversy. It is as much 
a matter of right for the plaintiffs to have the plaint correct 
by this amendment. 
The Rule confers a very wide discretion on courts in 
the matter of amendment of pleadings. As a general rule, 
leave to amend will be granted so as to enable the real 
question in issue between the parties to be raised in 
pleadings, where the amendment will occasion no injury 
to the opposite party and can be sufficiently compensated 
for by costs or other terms to be imposed by the order. In 
the case of Kishandas Rupchand and another Vs. 
Rachappa Vithoba Shilwant and others reported in  (1909)  
33 Bom 644) Batchelo, J observed that- 
 
“All amendments ought to be allowed, at any of 
the 
proceedings, 
which 
satisfy 
the 
two 
conditions (a) of not working injustice to the 
other side, and (b) of being necessary for the 
purpose of determining the real question in 
controversy between the parties.” 
 
Therefore, the main points to be considered before a 
party is allowed to amend his pleadings are, firstly, 
whether the amendment is necessary to determine the real 
question 
in 
controversy, 
and 
secondly, 
can 
the 
amendment be allowed without injustice to the other side? 
The first condition that must be satisfied before the Court 
can allow the amendment is whether such an amendment 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
is necessary to determine real questions in controversy. If 
that condition is not satisfied, the amendment should not 
be allowed. On the other hand, if the amendment is 
necessary to decide the “real controversy” between the 
parties, the amendment should be allowed even though 
the Court may think that the party seeking the 
amendment will not be able to prove the amended plea. 
This basic test governs the Courts’ unchartered powers of 
amendment, which should be allowed when it does not 
satisfy this cardinal test. Thus, it has been held that 
where the amendment is sought to avoid multiplicity of 
suits, or where the parties in the plaint are wrongly 
described, or where some facts are omitted from the plaint 
by inadvertence, or where there is a mistake in the 
statement of the case of action, or a bonafide omission in 
making the necessary averments in the plaint, or a suit is 
brought under a wrong Act. The amendment should be 
allowed. The second condition is also equally important, 
according to which no amendment will be allowed, which 
will cause injustice to the opposite party. It is a settled law 
that the amendment can be allowed if it can be without 
injustice to the other side. 
It appears that in an application for amendment 
after the commencement of trial, the applicant and the 
Court must write the cogent reason. However, the plain 
reading of the application under Order VI Rule 17 of the 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
instant case manifests that the proposed amendment 
admittedly changed the suit’s nature and character. 
Moreover, the reasons for the delay in the amendment 
application have not been adequately explained, and the 
appellate Court allowed the application without giving any 
cogent reasons. 
So, I believe that the Appeal Court committed an 
error of law, resulting in an error in the decision, 
occasioning a failure of justice in allowing the application 
for amendment of the plaint resulted in an error in the 
decision, occasioning a failure of justice. As such, the 
impugned judgment and order require interference by this 
Court.  
Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute without any 
order as to the costs. The impugned judgment and order 
dated 24.05.2023 passed by the learned Additional 
District Judge, 2nd Court, Munshiganj in Title Appeal 
No.140 of 2013 is hereby set aside. 
The order of stay passed at the time of issuance of 
the Rule is hereby vacated. 
Communicate the judgment at once.  
       ...……………………. 
(Md. Salim, J).

input_summary: The defendants in a title suit carried this revision against an order of the appellate court permitting the plaintiffs to amend their plaint. The plaintiffs had sued for declaration of title and lost in the trial court; while their appeal was pending they applied for amendment, and the appellate court acceded to it, observing that the amendment would not change the nature and character of the suit. The defendants contended that the application had come after the trial had commenced, that no satisfaction had been recorded that the matter could not have been raised earlier despite diligence, and that the proposed amendment altered the very character of the suit. The plaintiffs maintained that the court has wide power to allow amendment at any stage.
explanation: The court set out the terms of Order 6 rule 17 and the governing principles: an amendment necessary to decide the real question in controversy may be permitted at any stage provided it works no injustice to the opposite side, courts existing to do justice and not to punish parties for mistakes; but where amendment is sought after the trial has begun, both the applicant and the court must record cogent reasons. Applying that test, it found on a plain reading of the application that the proposed amendment admittedly changed the nature and character of the suit, that the delay was unexplained, and that no cogent reasons had been recorded. The order was interfered with and the stay vacated.

input_summary: The plaintiff in a title suit carried this revision after both the trial court and the first appellate court decided against him. He claimed title to a large area of land on the strength of a settlement said to have been taken from the manager of a waqf estate, followed by a registered sale in his favour, and complained that the land had erroneously been recorded in the government's name as forest land in the settlement and revisional records. The forest department contested the claim, asserting that the land had been made khas by notifications of the nineteen fifties and brought under forest management, and that there had been no settlement with the plaintiff's predecessor.
explanation: Examining the record, the court found that part of the plot belonged to persons who were not the landlords through whom the plaintiff claimed, so the alleged oral settlement by those landlords was manifestly without jurisdiction, and that neither a patta nor a kabuliyat was produced although the plaint's own sale deed mentioned one. The witness produced to vouch for the old rent receipts was not competent, having neither witnessed the settlement nor been born at the time. The court further held that the suit, asserting ignorance of the records until the mid-eighties while paying rent into the late eighties, disclosed a made-up cause of action and was barred by limitation, leaving the concurrent findings undisturbed.

khatian No. 148 of mouza Sangdia, police station  Kachua, distributed  
in several plots  admittedly belonged to  Baru Bibi the initial plaintiff.

Illiterate pardanisin rural woman Baru Bibi started running from earth 
to heaven. She filed an application to the then Sub-Divisional Officer

numbered as Title Suit No.386 of 1976 in the Court of the then Ist.

Admitted position is that:-

input_summary: The defendant in a suit for cancellation of a registered sale deed carried this revision against the appellate decree which decided the suit in the plaintiff's favour. The plaintiff, an elderly illiterate village woman observing seclusion, had gone to the sub-registrar's office intending to sell a small portion of her land to raise money for her ailing husband's treatment. Her case was that the deed was drafted by a scribe engaged by the purchaser and never read over or explained to her, that her entire holding was inserted in place of the small plot bargained for, and that she received no consideration at all, complaining to the revenue officer immediately afterwards.
explanation: The court noted the admitted position that the whole property belonged to the plaintiff, that she was an old illiterate woman observing seclusion, and that she had consistently, from the outset, objected to the transaction before the revenue officer and in an administrative inquiry. It observed that she had put only her thumb impression, consistent with her station, and that the person who identified her before the sub-registrar was of undisclosed responsibility and relationship, so the safeguard the law prescribes for a pardanashin woman had been overlooked. There was also no reliable evidence of payment of consideration, the administrative report recording dispute and confusion. The appellate findings were left undisturbed.

input_summary: The defendant in a small causes suit carried this revision against the decree passed against him, directing his eviction and recovery of arrears of rent. The landlord's case was that he had acquired the land by registered deeds, that his predecessor had let it out to the defendant for a long term, that a sawmill stood on it, and that the defendant had stopped paying the monthly rent agreed, a notice determining the tenancy having been served without compliance. The defendant denied default and asserted that he was depositing the rent regularly in a rent control proceeding of his own. His advocate was absent at the hearing.
explanation: The court heard the landlord's senior advocate and examined the plaint, the written statement, the evidence and the judgment of the small causes court. It found that the court had held the tenant to have failed to pay rent regularly and, more importantly, that although the tenant asserted he had been depositing monthly rent in a rent control case, he neither called for the records of that case nor produced any deposit receipt or order sheet to substantiate the claim. No illegality or error occasioning a failure of justice appearing, the court also observed that the revisional route chosen was incompetent, the proper course being the remedy the small causes statute itself provides. The rule failed.

input_summary: The defendants in a suit for a permanent injunction carried this revision after the appellate court decided the suit in the plaintiffs' favour, reversing the trial court. The plaintiffs traced title to a registered deed of the early nineteen seventies, asserting that the defendants had threatened to dispossess them, while the defendants produced their own deeds of a later period and a gift, together with the latest record of rights in their own name, and asserted that the deed relied on by the plaintiffs was fabricated. The trial court had decided against the plaintiffs, holding that they had failed to prove title, possession or even the threat complained of.
explanation: The court observed that in a suit for a permanent injunction the plaintiff must establish exclusive possession, the court being concerned only incidentally with prima facie title, and that where the dispute raises complicated questions of title a regular suit for declaration is the proper remedy, not an injunction suit used as a testing device. It found that the plaintiffs' witnesses could not specify the land or its boundaries, that none supported the alleged threat, and that both sides claimed the same land on the strength of registered deeds. The appellate court having reversed these findings without adverting to the evidence, the decree was overturned and the dismissal restored.

input_summary: The plaintiffs in a title suit over a large tract of land carried this revision against an order of the appellate court which had reversed the rejection of the defendants' application to reopen an ex parte decree passed against them years earlier. The defendants had asserted that no summons was ever served on their predecessor in interest, so they had no opportunity to contest the suit, and the appellate court restored the suit for trial, imposing costs. The plaintiffs maintained that the summons had in fact been served and signed for in the presence of the defendants' own sons, and that the decree was therefore sound.
explanation: The court noted the conflict between the two courts below, the trial court having accepted the service of summons and the appellate court having found material enabling the defendants to show non-service, and observed that an ex parte decree may be reopened under Order 9 rule 13 where sufficient cause for non-appearance is shown. It found that the appellate court had acted properly in restoring the suit on terms, and that the question of service was one to be decided by the trial court after evidence from both sides rather than in revision. It therefore declined to interfere and directed the suit to be concluded within a fixed period.

input_summary: The plaintiffs sued for specific performance of a contract of sale over a large tract of land, pleading that the owners had executed a written agreement in their favour, received part of the price and put them in possession, promising a registered deed after obtaining the necessary clearances, and that the vendors later left the country. The defendants denied execution of the agreement, asserting that it was a fabrication and that no money or possession had passed to the plaintiffs, and that the vendors had departed without arranging the management of their land. The trial court decided against the plaintiffs and the appellate court reversed that decision.
explanation: The court found that the agreement relied on, an unregistered document of the late nineteen sixties promising a sale, could not be treated as a valid instrument for transferring land, and that neither a patta nor possession in the plaintiffs was established, a witness produced to vouch for old rent receipts being incompetent. It held that a suit to enforce such a contract must be brought within the period prescribed by article 113 of the Limitation Act 1908, computed from refusal to execute the deed, and that no believable evidence of such refusal existed. The suit having come nearly ten years after the agreement, the trial court's findings were restored.

explanation: The court observed that under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the right depends on the relative dates of registration, a deed being treated as registered once it is entered in the volumes of the registry office, and that neither side produced those volumes to show which entry came first. input_summary: Two partition proceedings between the same parties over the same land were carried to this court by the district council, which complained that the courts below had allotted shares to the contesting plaintiffs alone although the record itself acknowledged that the council and other public bodies held portions of the land, and that no share at all had been carved out for them or for the other added parties. The council placed additional papers before this court to support its claim. The plaintiffs maintained that they alone had proved their case and that the others had produced no document.
explanation: The court noted that the contesting plaintiffs had proved title to part of the land, and that both courts below had expressly recognised that the council had purchased a parcel and that other bodies and added parties also had interests there. Despite that, the preliminary decree allotted shares only to the plaintiffs, leaving the acknowledged interests of the remaining parties undetermined, so the partition was incomplete. Since the other claimants had never had a proper opportunity to prove their shares, the court reversed both decrees, remanded the proceedings for a fresh hearing with liberty to adduce further documents, and directed the parties to maintain the existing position meanwhile.

Turning to the development cost, it found the purchaser's claim of a large sum unsupported, while the commissioner's valuation of ninety-two thousand rupees was on the low side, and it settled a reasonable figure of one lakh fifteen thousand rupees on the basis of the current market value. The rule was disposed of with that modification alone, the pre-emptor being directed to pay that sum within three months and the purchasers to execute the deed.

input_summary: The plaintiffs lost their title suit, and their appeal was heard and decided on the very day the record reached the appellate judge, without acceding to the defendants' prayer for an adjournment. The defendants then applied to have the appeal reheard, and the appellate judge restored it, undoing the judgment already pronounced. The plaintiffs challenged that restoration here, arguing that the application was not competent because it sought restoration of the appeal only and not of the decree, and that no proper hearing had been given before the appeal was decided in the defendants' absence.
explanation: The court examined the course followed below and observed that the appeal had been taken up and disposed of on the day the file was received, without deciding the defendants' prayer for time, and that such haste was not consistent with the requirement that a case be heard on both sides. It nevertheless found that the provision invoked, Order 41 rule 21A of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, empowers an appellate court to rehear an appeal decided in a party's absence, and that the application had been made within the time prescribed. The restoration order being in accordance with law, the rule failed, with a direction to rehear the appeal within a fixed period.

input_summary: The husband in a family suit carried this revision against the concurrent orders directing him to pay dower and maintenance to his wife and their minor daughter. His case was that dower had been fixed at a lesser figure than the amount recorded in the marriage document, which he said had been altered by forgery, and that he had pronounced divorce by affidavit, so the wife was no longer entitled to maintenance. The wife asserted that the marriage document was genuine and that the alleged divorce had not been effected in accordance with the prescribed procedure. He also pleaded inability to pay at once.
explanation: The court found from the record that the marriage was admitted, that the daughter was born of the union, and that no procedure prescribed for effecting a divorce had been followed, so the husband's assertion of divorce was not made out; both courts had concurrently so held. The decree for dower and maintenance, and the monthly amounts fixed for the wife and the daughter, therefore stood. The only indulgence given was as to payment: accepting that the husband had limited means, the court permitted him to discharge the decretal amount in six equal monthly instalments, the execution case to proceed if he defaulted.

explanation: The court considered the power of a commissioner appointed in a partition suit to measure and demarcate the shares of the respective parties, and held that the commissioner is competent to report on the land actually available, a variance between the decretal quantity and the area found on survey not by itself vitiating the report. input_summary: In a small causes suit for eviction and arrears of rent, the defendant denied the tenancy agreement relied on by the landlord and asserted that his signature on it was not his, and applied at a late stage of the trial for the signature to be examined by a handwriting expert. Both the trial court and the revisional court below turned the application down, the revisional court taking the view that the request was made with a view to delaying the case. The defendant carried that rebuff to this court, contending that an expert opinion was necessary for a just decision.
explanation: The court noted that the application had come at an advanced stage of a long-pending suit and agreed that the delay was not satisfactorily explained, so the refusal of an expert opinion at that stage was not unreasonable. It nonetheless considered that where the genuineness of a signature is in issue the court has power under section 45 of the Evidence Act 1872 to obtain the opinion of an expert, and that refusing the request outright could prejudice a proper decision. It therefore disposed of the rule with directions: the defendant may arrange and pay for an expert, applying afresh, and the suit is to be concluded within three months.

input_summary: The plaintiff sued for a declaration that a registered testamentary instrument executed by his father over the family land was illegal and not binding on him, pleading that it had been made in favour of all the successors, that he learned of it only when his brother sought to sell part of the property, and that the testator had himself later sold a portion, showing the instrument had been abandoned. The defendants, the other successors, maintained that the instrument was validly executed and registered in accordance with the personal law governing them.
explanation: The court considered the instrument, its registration and the scheme of distribution it laid down, and observed that under the personal law applicable to the parties an owner may dispose of his property among his children and grandchildren, and may do so by an instrument taking effect after his death. It found that the plaintiff was one of the beneficiaries named in it and that a specific share had been allotted to him, and that both courts below had concurrently held the instrument operative and the plaintiff not entitled to the declaration he sought. No error of law appearing, the court declined to interfere.

The defendants, one of whom is the petitioner here, contended that the property had descended differently, that the plaintiff had no share in it, and that the suit was in any event barred by lapse of time, the deed having been executed many years earlier and signed by the plaintiff's own husband. Both courts below decided the suit in the plaintiff's favour.
explanation: The court examined the provision of the Limitation Act 1908 fixing a short period, computed from knowledge, for a suit to cancel an instrument, and found that the plaint asserted knowledge only in the closing months before filing, a matter spoken to in evidence, so the plea of bar by time was not sustained. It noted that the two plots in question had been shown in the partition deed although the plaintiff was not a party to it, that no party had proved otherwise, and that the appellate court had concurrently found the inclusion of her land illegal. The additional documents sought to be produced at the appellate stage came too late and rested on no proper foundation.

input_summary: The plaintiffs sued for declaration of title and confirmation of possession over a parcel of land, pleading that a purchase made in the nineteen forties had in truth been made with their predecessor's money in another man's name, and that a revenue sale and auction purchase relied on by the defendants were collusive and never took place. The defendants asserted that the purchaser of the deed had bought with his own funds, that the record stood in his name, and that on default of rent the land was auctioned and possession delivered through court to the auction purchasers, whose successors they are. The trial court decided against the plaintiffs, and the appellate court reversed that.
explanation: The court examined the deed itself and found it executed in the sole name of the purchaser, containing nothing to indicate that anyone else had an interest in the transaction, and it set out the recognised tests for identifying a benami purchase, including custody of the document, the source of the money, the purpose and the possession; none of them was satisfied on the plaintiffs' evidence. It further found that the revenue sale for arrears, the auction purchase and the delivery of possession through the process server were all proved by the defence papers, and that the possession of the plaintiffs' predecessors was not made out. The appellate court's reversal being unsound, the trial court's decision was restored.

input_summary: The defendants in a partition suit carried this revision against a decree allocating shares to the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs claimed title and partition of a parcel tracing descent from the original recorded owner through his widow, daughter and four nephews, and complained that the record of rights had been wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants' predecessors. The defendants asserted that the original owner had died unmarried, that only his four nephews inherited him, and that a sale deed of the nineteen thirties, later inherited through several hands, gave them title. The trial court decided against the plaintiffs; the appellate court decreed partition with specific shares.
explanation: The court observed that the two sides advanced long and conflicting genealogies, the single point of difference being whether the original owner died leaving a widow and a daughter in addition to his nephews. It found that the trial court had not addressed the plaintiffs' evidence of descent and had failed to allocate any shares at all, although a court trying a title and partition suit is obliged to do so on the basis of title and possession. The appellate court, on the other hand, had sifted the depositions of the witnesses produced by both sides and allotted defined shares to the respective branches, a course the record supported. No error of law being shown, the decree stood.

input_summary: The plaintiff sued for declaration of title over a parcel of land, tracing it back to a purchase by a former landlord in the late nineteen thirties and a settlement two years later, followed by several transfers ending with an exchange deed in his favour. He complained that the revenue office had declined to accept rent because the land was not recorded in his predecessor's name. The government contested the suit, asserting that a portion of the plots remained unrecorded and had been settled with other persons, and that part of the land stood listed as vested property. Both courts below decided against the plaintiff.
explanation: The court examined the plaint and the documents and found that the land had been described in the plaint without any boundary and without a definite identification, the plaintiff himself being uncertain as to which portion belonged to him, and that the two portions of the plot concerned had not even been identified by dag numbers. It further found that other necessary parties had been left out, and that a suit of this kind, entailing the ascertainment of several shares, should have been framed as one for partition. The evidence of the plaintiff's witness was held to establish neither title nor possession. Both courts having so found, the concurrent findings were left undisturbed.

input_summary: The defendants in a partition suit carried this revision after both courts below protected the plaintiffs' possession by an interim order pending trial. The plaintiffs sued for partition of land in which they claimed shares by purchase and by inheritance, and applied for a temporary injunction, pleading that they cultivated part of the land and that fishery land of theirs had been merged into a flood control embankment, and that they had been seeking a lease of the water area from the authorities. The defendant, an office-bearer of a body of beneficiaries of a re-excavation project, opposed the prayer. The government contested the suit without meeting the injunction application.
explanation: The court noted that the trial court had examined the plaintiffs' documents and found their possession of the land shown to it, and that the appellate court had confirmed that finding. It observed with some concern that the land in question lay within the control of the water development authorities and that neither the district administration nor any other government office had given the court any real assistance, despite the court asking the Attorney General's office for submissions. Nothing being shown against the concurrent findings on the interlocutory application, and the usual considerations governing interim protection having been addressed, the court declined to interfere.

input_summary: The appellant was convicted of dishonouring a cheque drawn to discharge a liability, which came back unpaid for insufficiency of funds after the complainant had completed all the statutory steps, and was sentenced to a year's simple imprisonment and a fine. In this appeal his advocate stated at the outset that the appellant had since settled the matter by paying the complainant the full value of the cheque, and asked the court to act on the compromise; the complainant's advocate concurred in that request. The matter therefore turned on whether a composition could be given effect after conviction.
explanation: The court pointed out that the offence created by the special statute is not compoundable, so that a private settlement cannot by itself efface a conviction recorded on evidence. It turned to an apex court decision in which, a compromise having been reached with half the cheque money paid in cash and the balance deposited in court, the sentence was reduced to the term already served and the complainant was permitted to withdraw the deposit. Applying that approach to the present case, the court left the conviction where it stood but reduced the substantive sentence to the period already undergone, and directed the trial court to release the amount deposited in favour of the complainant.

Both accused were sentenced to six months' imprisonment and a fine. explanation: The court held that the offence belongs to the class which the statute does not permit to be compounded, and that the prayer for wiping out the conviction altogether could not therefore be acceded to merely because money had changed hands after the verdict. It referred to an apex court ruling in which a post-conviction compromise had been given effect by trimming the sentence to the period already undergone and by releasing the deposited sum to the complainant, and adopted the same course. The appeal was thus brought to an end with the sentence reduced to the term already served and a direction to the trial court to release the money.

suit for declaration that the creation of the case record, the kabuliyat 
deed and the khatian showing settlement of 60 decimal land of Plot

landless peasant by registered kabuliyat dated 05.01.2002 and plaintiff 
is in possession in the same by constructing dwelling house. The 
plaintiff came to know that defendant Nos.4 and 5 in collusion with the 
Officers of the local Assistant Commissioner Land Office has created 
collusive and fabricated khatian and kabuliyat showing settlement of 60 
decimal land out of above Plot No.662 in favour of defendant No.4 and 
5.  
The suit was contested by defendant No.1 Government of 
Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commission, Noakhali and 
defendant Nos.4 and 5 by filing separate written statement wherein 
they have denied all claims set out in the plaint and stated that on 
compliance of relevant rules and procedure 60 decimal land has been 
given settlement to landless peasants defendant No.4 and 5 and they 
are in peaceful possession in the same.  
On conclusion of trial the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the 
suit and being aggrieved by above judgment and decree of trial Court 
plaintiffs preferred Civil Appeal No.86 of 2017 to the District Judge 
which was transferred to the learned Additional District Judge for 
hearing.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
In above appeal appellant filed a petition on 20.02.2022 for 
amendment of the plaint for inclusion of a relief for declaration of title 
in above land.

respective parties and materials on record the learned Additional 
District Judge rejected above petition vide impugned order dated 
19.06.2023.

Judge of the Court of appeal below above appellants as petitioners 
moved to this Court and obtained this Rule.

submits that the petitioners as plaintiffs instituted above suit under 
Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 for a negative declaration that 
the kabuliyat, and settlement case showing settlement of 60 decimal of 
land of the disputed plot to defendant Nos.4 and 5 is unlawful and not 
binding upon the plaintiff. At appeal the appellant merely wanted to 
incorporate a further declaration of his title since his title was clouded.

the suit but the learned Additional District Judge has misconceived 
above facts and relevant laws and most illegally rejected above petition 
for amendment of the plaint which is not tenable in law.

previously instituted Title Suit No.26 of 1981 against the same 
defendants for declaration of title for selfsame land in the 1st Court of

such the issues of this suit between this parties were conclusively and

same cause against the same defendants which is not tenable in law.

and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 29.09.2021 passed

suit should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or 
orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 
 
Facts in short are that  opposite party as plaintiff instituted  above 
Family Suit for recovery of her unpaid dower of Taka 1,50,000/- and 
maintenance alleging that the defendant married her on 02.06.2007 by a 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
registered kabinnama and subsequently subjected the plaintiff to 
physical and psychological torture on demand of dowry. Due to 
plaintiffs refusal to pay dowry the defendant divorced the plaintiff on 
30.06.2018.  
 
Defendant contested above suit by filing a written statement 
alleging that the dower of the plaintiff was fixed at Taka 50,000/- and

plaintiff has fraudulently enhanced the dower to Taka 2,00,000/-. The 
plaintiff having involved in immoral and antisocial activities the 
defendant has divorced her on 30.06.2018. The defendant purchased 
sanchoypatra of Taka 40,000/- in the name of the plaintiff which may 
be utilized for payment of her maintenance.

the document of the plaintiff was marked as Exhibit No.1 and that of 
the defendant was marked as Exhibit No.Ka.

suit and granted plaintiff unpaid dower of Taka 1,50,000/- and 
maintenance at the rate of Taka 3,500/- from 19.03.2018.

Court the defendant preferred Family Appeal No.03 of 2022 to the 
learned District Judge, Jhalakathi who dismissed above appeal and 
affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

3

hearing on several dates.

submits that the registered kabinnama of the plaintiff was produced at 
trial which was marked as Exhibit No.1. Above document shows that 
the dower of the plaintiff was fixed at Taka 2,00,000/- and only Taka
