is reasonable and bearable for the defendant. On consideration of above 
evidence on record the learned District Judge has rightly dismissed the 
appeal and upheld the judgment and decree of the Family Court which 
calls for interference.    
 
I have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for 
the opposite party and carefully examined all materials on record.  
 
It is admitted that the defendant married the plaintiff on 
02.06.2007 by a registered kabinnama and above marriage came to one 
end by talak on 30.06.2018 at the instance of the defendant.  

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4

plaintiff was entitled to get Taka 1,50,000-/ as unpaid dower.  
The learned Judges of the Courts below have granted past 
maintenance to the plaintiff from 19.03.2018. But the plaintiff did not 
mention in her evidence as PW1 that she was living separately from the 
defendant from 19.03.2018 and the defendant did not pay her 
maintenance from above date. As such the plaintiff has failed to 
substantiate her claim for past maintenance by legal evidence.  
The monthly maintenance of the plaintiff at the rate of Taka 
3,500/- as was determined by the learned Judges of the Courts below 
appears to be reasonable taking into account the existing market price 
and other expenses of a divorcee woman living separately and alone.

entitled to get maintenance at the rate of Taka 3,5000/- only for his 
iddat period which amounts to Taka 11,900/-.

evidence of the record I am of the view that the ends of the justice of 
will be met if the impugned judgment and decree is modified and

5
above suit is decreed for Taka 1,61,900/ (Taka 1,50,000/- for unpaid

judgment and decree dated 29.09.2021 passed by the Bicharak, Rajapur 
Family Court and Senior Assistant Judge, Rajapur Court, Jhalakathi in 
Family Suit No.34 of 2018 is upheld subject to modification of the 
decree to Taka 1,61,900/- instead of Taka 1,92,400/-. 
 
This Rule is accordingly disposed of.  
 
Send down the lower Courts records immediately. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MD. MASUDUR RAHMAN

input_summary: The wife sued her former husband in the family court for unpaid dower and maintenance, pleading that they had married by a registered marriage document, that he had ill-treated her over demands for money, and that he divorced her in the middle of the year two thousand eighteen. He asserted that the dower had in fact been fixed at a much smaller sum which he had paid in full, that it had been inflated in the document by fraud, and that investments he had made in her name could meet her maintenance. The family court decreed dower and maintenance, and the appeal confirmed that. His advocate did not appear here.
explanation: The court found the registered marriage document to show the dower at the agreed higher figure with only part of it paid, so the unpaid balance was due; the marriage itself and its dissolution were admitted. Turning to maintenance, it observed that the wife had not stated in her evidence that she had lived apart from the husband from the date she claimed, nor that nothing had been paid to her, so the arrears claimed for the past were not established. The monthly rate fixed below was held reasonable, but since the marriage had ended in divorce, she was entitled to that rate only for the period of waiting, and the decree was reduced accordingly.

issuance of the Rule on 30.04.1989. Under the order of Hon’ble

contending, inter-alia, that the suit land appertaining to C.S.

Company Limited. The father of the plaintiff took settlement of

operation the suit land was recorded in the Khas Khatian and upon 
getting the information about wrong recording in the year 1385

contending, inter-alia, that the suit land was belonged to 
Medenipur Zamindar and after operation of the State Acquisition 
and Tenancy Act, the property has been vested to the Government.

accordingly, the name of Government in S.A. khatian was rightly 
recorded. The plaintiff has no right, title and possession over the 
suit land.

Heard on: 30.10.2024

Rule was issued on an application under section 115 of the 
Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1-8 
to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 
03.07.1989 passed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Magura in Title 
Appeal No. 17 of 1988 affirming those of dated 28.12.1987 
passed by the Assistant Judge, Mohammadpur, Magura in Title 
Suit No. 778 of 1984 should not be set aside and/or such other or 
further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
The present petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 525 
of 1981 before the Court of First Munsif, Magura subsequently on 
transfer the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 778 of 1984 and 
was heard by the Upazila Munsif, Mohammadpur, Magura, 
wherein the plaintiff sought for declaration of title and 
confirmation of possession contending, inter-alia, that the suit 
land was originally belonged to Kazem Shaik; Kasimuddin got the 
property through settlement from the aforesaid Kazem Shaik and 
thereby enjoying the property peacefully. Kasimuddin died 
intestate leaving behind a son Tasiruddin, who inherited his 
paternal property. Thereafter on 23.11.1959 Tasiruddin transferred 
the property to Saleha Khatoon wife of plaintiff No. 1 and mother 
of plaintiff Nos. 2-5 through registered kabala dated 23.11.1959. 
Saleha Khatoon died intestate leaving behind the plaintiffs as legal 
heirs. Plaintiffs are in possession in the suit land. The defendants 
have no title or possession into the suit land. The defendants 
threatened the plaintiffs to dispossess denying their title into the 
land on 10.11.1981 and upon such cause of action the plaintiffs 
instituted the suit. 
The defendant Nos. 1-8 contested the suit by filing written 
statement denying all the material averments of the plaint 
contending, inter-alia, that the suit land was originally belonged 
to Kazem Shaik; while Kazem Shaik was in peaceful possession 
and enjoyment of the suit property died intestate leaving behind 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
only son Falu Shaik as legal heir. Falu Shaik transferred the 
property to Narendra Nath Basu by registered kabala dated 
07.11.1959. Subsequently, the said Narendra Nath Basu 
transferred 25 decimals of land from the suit property to Abdul 
Gani and Gafur Mollah by registered kabala dated 28.11.1962. 
Gafur Molla died intestate leaving behind defendant Nos. 1-3 as 
his legal heirs and Abdul Gani Molla died intestate leaving behind 
defendant Nos. 4-8 as his legal heirs. Narendra nath Basu also 
transferred the rest 37 decimals of land to defendant No. 1 and 
inducted him into the possession, but due to insufficient fund the 
said defendant could not get the kabala registered. The plaintiffs 
have no right, title possession over the suit land and as such the 
suit is liable to be dismissed.  
During hearing the plaintiffs examined 3(three) witnesses 
and adduced documentary evidences and exhibited kabala dated 
23.11.1959 as Exhibit-‘Ka’ and ‘Khazna Dakhilas’ as Exhibit-
‘Kha-series’. On the other hand, the defendants also examined 
3(three) witnesses and exhibited 2(two) kabalas dated 7.11.1959 
(Exhibit-1) and kabala dated 28.11.1962 (Exhibit-2).  
On conclusion of hearing learned Judge of the trial Court by 
his judgment and decree dated 28.12.1987 dismissed the suit, on 
the findings that the plaintiffs’ suit is barred by limitation, hit by 
section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and the plaintiffs also 
failed to prove their title over the suit land. 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
Having been aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and 
decree dated 28.12.1987, the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal No. 
17 of 1998 before the District Judge, Magura, which on transfer 
ultimately heard by the Sub-ordinate Judge, Magura and learned 
Sub-ordinate Judge by his judgment and decree dated 03.07.1989 
dismissed the appeal affirming those of the trial Court. 
On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid 
judgment dated 03.07.1989 of the Sub-ordinate Judge, Magura, 
the plaintiffs-petitioners filed this revisional application and 
obtained the Rule. 
Mr. Bivash Chandra Biswas, learned Senior Advocate 
appearing for the petitioners submits that the Court of appeal 
below failed to discuss all the evidences on record and thereby 
arrived at any independent findings as per Order XLI, rule 31 of 
the Code of Civil Procedure. He next submits that the Exhibit-
‘Kha series’ proved the chain of title of the plaintiffs, the 
defendants even did not challenge the dakhilas as forged and 
created, thus, the dakhilas stand. He further submits that if it is 
proved that the title of the property was transferred to Tasiruddin 
from Kazem Shaik through settlement, thus the predecessor of the 
defendants, named Falu Shaik would be title less person and in 
that case Exhibit-‘1’ and ‘2’, the deeds dated 07.11.1959 and 
28.11.1962 would be baseless and conferred no title upon the 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
defendants. He continues to submit that if the settlement is not 
proved then the defendants could have a case. 
 
He again submits that the plaintiffs-appellants on 
10.04.1989 filed an application sought for sending back the suit on 
remand to the trial Court contending, inter-alia, that the plaintiffs 
with due diligence could not produce the registered kabuliyats, the 
basic documents of settlement, dated 12.06.1925 and 11.01.1927. 
On 31.01.1988 and 22.02.1988, they could manage to obtain the 
certified copies of those kabuliyats and now through the 
application they were filing those documents and thereby prayed 
for sending back the case on remand. The Court of appeal below 
failed to deal with the said application in accordance with law and 
thereafter, before this Court the plaintiffs-petitioners by way of 
supplementary affidavit submitted certified copies of those 
kabuliyats. In such facts and circumstances he sought for sending 
back the case on remand for ends of justice to enable the 
petitioners to establish their title over the suit land. 
 
On the other hand, Mr. A.H.M Obaidul Kabir, learned 
Advocate appearing for the opposite-party Nos. 1-8 submits that 
both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs 
miserably failed to prove their title and exclusive possession over 
the suit land. The concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the 
Courts below upon proper appreciation of the evidences on record 
is immune from interference in revision. He next submits that the 

<<PAGE 6>>
6 
 
plaintiffs failed to prove exclusive possession over the suit land 
and thus, the suit for declaration of title and confirmation of 
possession is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. He 
further submits that the dakhilas or related documents, the basic 
title documents of the plaintiffs having not been proved in 
accordance with law. He also submits that the application filed by 
the plaintiffs-appellants-petitioners before the appellate Court 
below on 10.04.1989 was not pressed before the Court concerned, 
even at the argument stage or any time before pronouncement of 
judgment and accordingly, the appellate Court below has come to 
a positive finding that the appellants are not entitled to get any 
remedy through the aforesaid application and now, the plaintiffs-
petitioners cannot be allowed to agitate the same prayer before the 
revisional Court, because they are barred by Estoppel. He further 
submits that the order of remand cannot be allowed as a matter of 
course to fill up the lacuna of plaintiffs’ case, thus, the prayer for 
remand to fill up the lacuna cannot not be allowed legally at this 
revisional stage. In support of his submission, he referred the case 
of Abdus Sobhan Vs. Anwar Rahim and others reported in 53 
DLR(AD) 110, the case of Md. Abdus Satter and others Vs. Lalon 
Mazar Sharif and Seba Sadan Committee and others reported in 
24 BLD(AD) 125, the case of A.K.M Abu Sayed Chowdhury Vs. 
A.K.M Abdul Wahed Chowdhury and others reported in 64 DLR 
298. 

<<PAGE 7>>
7 
 
 
Heard learned Advocate of both the parties, perused the 
revisional application, the supplementary affidavit filed on behalf 
of the petitioners, having gone through the cited judgments and 
lower Courts’ record. 
 
It appears that the plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration of 
title and confirmation of possession, contending that their 
predecessor-in-interest, named Kasiruddin took settlement of 62 
decimals of land from one Kazem Shaik. It is evident from the 
record that the plaintiffs could not prove the aforesaid settlement, 
through the basic document of their title by adducing any 
evidence, oral or documentary before both the Courts below. As a 
result, the suit was dismissed, against which they took Title 
Appeal No. 17 of 1988, ultimately which was heard by the Sub-
ordinate Judge, Magura. During pendency of the appeal on 
10.04.1989, they filed an application before the appellate Court 
below sought for sending back the case on remand to the trial 
Court. Thereafter, on the occasion of 28.05.1989 the plaintiffs-
appellants took adjournment by filing an application. Thereafter, 
on 28.06.1989 the appellants placed their argument at length, but 
surprisingly they did not press the application dated 10.04.1989. 
Thereafter, on 03.07.1989, the appellate Court below delivered it’s 
judgment and rejected the said application stating that the 
plaintiffs-appellants did not press the application for unknown 

<<PAGE 8>>
8 
 
reason and as such, the application for sending back the case on 
remand cannot be considered.  
 
More so, it is the specific findings of learned Assistant 
Judge that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession over the 
suit land and the defendants are in possession into the suit land 
and as such, without having any prayer of consequential remedy 
under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 
praying for recovery of possession, the suit for declaration of title 
and confirmation of possession is not maintainable and hit by 
section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. The appellate Court 
below concurred with the aforesaid findings to the effect that the 
defendants are also in possession in the suit property.  
The proviso to the section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 
1877 contemplated that the plaintiffs are to sue for all reliefs 
which can possibly be granted, but where the consequential relief 
is found necessary, but has not been asked for; omission to sought 
for the said consequential relief makes the suit not maintainable. 
 In the present case, the plaintiffs are found out of 
possession of the suit land and at the same time, the defendants are 
found to be in possession over the said land. In such facts and 
circumstance, without having prayer of recovery of possession, 
the suit for mere declaration and confirmation of possession is not 
maintainable and in such situation, remanding back the case to the 

<<PAGE 9>>
9 
 
Court of original jurisdiction is amount to allow the plaintiffs to 
fill up their lacuna. 
Moreover, in no point of time, the plaintiffs filed an 
application sought for adducing additional evidences under the  
relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, rather opted to 
file an application before the appellate Court below on 10.04.1989 
sought for sending back the case on remand, but thereafter, they 
did not pursue or place the said application and accordingly, at 
time of pronouncement of judgment the appellate Court below 
came to the specific finding that the application cannot be 
entertained and rejected as not pressed. 
Through supplementary affidavit dated 31.03.1990 the 
plaintiffs-petitioners submitted certified copies of 2(two) 
kabuliyats. And now prayed for remanding back the case on 
remand again without having any explanation what so ever for not 
placing or pursuing the application dated 10.04.1989. And in view 
of above, the plaintiffs-petitioners are not allowed to submit the 
identical application again with identical prayer, which was 
rejected earlier by the appellate Court below for the allegation of 
not pressed. 
In the premise above, I do not find any reason to interfere 
into the concurrent findings of fact of both Courts below as to the 
title and regarding possession of the suit land. Moreover, the suit 

<<PAGE 10>>
10 
 
is not maintainable, hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 
1877.  
In view of above, this Court finds no reason to interfere into 
the judgment of the Courts below. 
Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to 
cost. 
Send down the lower Courts’ record.  
Communicate the judgment and order at once. 
 
 
 
 
 
Obaidul Hasan/B.O.

explanation: The court examined the rival chains and the documents, and agreed that the plaintiffs had not proved their title, that the suit was barred by time and that it was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. It explained the proviso to that section: a plaintiff must seek every relief open to him, and where the consequential relief of possession was necessary but not asked for, a suit confined to a bare declaration with confirmation of possession cannot stand. It added that the plaintiffs, being out of possession while the defendants held the land, could not be helped by a remand, which would only let them fill up gaps; the later documents were no answer.

daughter of Hasan Mondol, the admitted co-owners of the said

minors’ property in favour of the plaintiff through registered deed

defendants have no possession in the suit land.

minors property. Thus, the said deed does not confer any valid 
title upon the plaintiff and on the basis of the said finding he 
dismissed the suit.

plaintiff did not acquire any title into the suit land through the 
invalid or void registered deed dated 24.09.1958, but did not at all 
disturb or controvert the specific findings of the trial Court to the 
effect that the plaintiff is in possession and the defendants have 
not possession in the suit land. Thus, the finding of fact of the trial 
Court regarding possession of the plaintiff stands and which 
continues uninterruptedly from the execution of the deed of the 
year 1958. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act, 1908, the title 
of the legal owner of the property would be extinguished for his 
failure to claim or exercise his right or title over a period more 
than 12(twelve) years from the date of discontinuation of 
possession or in case of minors 3(three) years after attainment of

their behalf, but failed to consider that on  the strength of the said

date of their attainment of majority, whichever is later.

Limitation Act, 1908.

plaintiff did not specifically sought for the declaration of title by

issuance of the Rule is hereby recalled.

input_summary: The plaintiff sued for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and a permanent injunction over land he had bought in the late nineteen fifties and part of which he had later sold, placing reliance on a deed executed on his behalf by the vendors' elder brother as guardian and on long, uninterrupted possession. The defendant relied on an oral settlement in his favour and on a registered sale to him in the mid-seventies, supported by his own witnesses. The trial court decreed the suit, and the appellate court reversed that on the footing that the guardian had no authority to convey the minors' property.
explanation: The trial court had found the plaintiff in possession and the defendant out of it, a finding the appellate court left alone and the defendant left it unchallenged. Building on that, the court held that although the deed of the late fifties was invalid, the guardian having no power to convey the minors' interest, the plaintiff had held the land for far more than the statutory period. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act 1908 the title of the rightful owner is extinguished once that period runs out, so the plaintiff had gained title by adverse possession, and the vendors had lost theirs before selling to the defendant in the seventies. The plaint had also asserted such a title.

input_summary: The plaintiff, claiming to be the lawful custodian of a shrine and its endowed estate, sued for a declaration of that status, for a declaration that a letter of the endowment administrator inviting proposals for constituting a committee was unlawful, and for a declaration that the administrator's acceptance of subscriptions from the contesting defendant was likewise unlawful. Certain defendants applied for rejection of the plaint, contending that the civil court had no jurisdiction because the endowment statute bars such suits and provides an appeal against removal. The trial court and the revisional court below both declined to throw out the plaint.
explanation: The court examined the provisions of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 relied on and found that they operate where the administrator removes a custodian, the remedy being an appeal to the district judge. It observed that all suits of a civil nature lie before the civil courts unless a statute excludes that jurisdiction, that an exclusion is construed strictly, and that the burden of showing ouster lies on the party asserting it. Since the plaintiff had not been removed and no relief had been sought against any order of removal, the bar did not apply; the suit was one to enforce the rights attached to an office and was therefore of a civil nature and triable by the civil court.

the opposite parties submits that without fulfilling the criterion of 
Order XXIII, rule 1 and 2, the plaintiff is not entitled to withdraw 
his suit with permission to sue afresh. When the Court invites Mr. 
Ahmed’s attention to the application for withdrawal of the appeal 
as well as the suit filed by the plaintiff-appellant before the 
appellate Court below, wherefrom it transpires that the application 
was for withdrawal of the appeal as well as the suit simplicitor 
without any further prayer allowing him to sue afresh on the self 
same cause of action. i.e. The plaintiff did not apply before the 
Court for seeking further permission to sue afresh. Then, Mr. 
Ahmed did not show his willingness to make further argument.  

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
Heard learned Advocates for both the parties, perused the 
revisional application together with the annexures. 
It appears that sub-rule (1) of rule 1 of Order XXIII of the 
Code of Civil Procedure provides that at any time after institution 
of the suit the plaintiff may withdraw his suit or abandon part of 
his claim. Meaning thereby, the aforesaid provision of sub-rule (1) 
does not impose any bar or restriction upon the plaintiff to 
withdraw his suit simplicitor, which includes withdrawal of appeal 
also i.e. the plaintiff or appellant, as the case may be, is entitled to 
withdraw his suit or appeal simplicitor at any time after institution 
of the suit, without seeking further permission to sue afresh on the 
self same cause of action, provided that in case of appeal, the 
respondent has not acquired any interest under the judgment and 
decree of the trial Court. Meaning thereby, the plaintiff-appellant 
can withdraw his suit as a matter of right and the Court has no 
option but to allow his application of withdrawal the appeal as 
well as the suit simplicitor. 
In the case of Baidyanath Nandi Vs. Shyama Sundar Nandi 
reported in A.I.R.(30) 1943 (Cal) 427.  It was held that “If he does 
not want the liberty to institute a fresh suit nor seeks to avoid the 
consequences which sub-rule (3) imposes upon him he can 
withdraw the suit suo motu as laid down in sub-rule (1).” Thus, 
the plaintiff’s application for withdrawal of the suit should be 
allowed as a matter of right. 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
In the premise above, this Court finds merit in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 
The order dated 11.03.2019 is hereby set aside and the 
plaintiff-petitioner is hereby allowed to withdraw his appeal as 
well as the suit simplicitor, provided further that according to the 
sub-rule (3), the plaintiff-petitioner shall not be entitled to sue 
again on the same cause of action. According to the judgment of 
the Apex Court passed in the case of Abdur Rahman and others 
Vs. Kheru Malitha and others reported in 50 DLR(AD)71, the 
withdrawal of a suit necessarily blots out the effect of the 
judgment and decree passed prior to the withdrawal. And as such, 
the judgment and decree dated 30.09.2015 passed by the Assistant 
Judge, Debhata, Satkhira in Title Suit No. 53 of 2011 is hereby set 
aside. 
No order as to cost.  
Communicate the judgment and order at once. 
 
 
 
 
Obaidul Hasan/B.O.
input_summary: The plaintiff sued for declaration of title and recovery of possession and lost on contest. He then applied to the appellate court, where his appeal was pending, seeking leave to withdraw the appeal as well as the suit outright. The appellate judge permitted him to withdraw the appeal but declined to let him withdraw the suit itself, leaving the decree of the trial court standing. The plaintiff carried that order to this court, asserting that a plaintiff may abandon his suit as of right where he seeks no liberty to sue afresh.
explanation: The court read the relevant rule of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 and found that its first sub-rule, which allows a plaintiff at any time after institution of the suit to withdraw it or to abandon part of his claim, imposes no restriction on an outright withdrawal, and that an appellant may similarly withdraw his appeal where the respondent has acquired no interest under the decree. It relied on a decision of the Calcutta High Court to the effect that where no liberty to sue afresh is wanted, the suit may be withdrawn of one's own motion. The order confining the withdrawal to the appeal was therefore undone, and the trial decree ceased to have effect.

on the mere ground that at a later stage the petitioner considered 

<<PAGE 14>>
14 
 
that the previous order is wrong or not in accordance with law; 
because, once the Court passed a decree, it becomes functus 
officio.  
The contention of Mr. Tariqul Islam, learned Advocate for 
the petitioner seems to be meritorious, but such criticism should 
be advanced not before the Court under the form of review 
application, but before a higher Court in appeal or revision under 
sections 96 or 115 of the Code (Revision against the judgment and 
decree of the appellate Court). Jurisdiction of review does not 
depend upon a strong or meritorious argument.  
The parameters to invoke the jurisdiction of review are 
specifically prescribed in Order XLVII of the Code of Civil 
Procedure. The former part of the rule deals with a situation 
attributable to the applicant, and the latter to a jural action, which 
is manifestly incorrect or illegal or on which two conclusions are 
not legally possible. Neither of them provide any scope of 
rehearing of the dispute a new to the petitioner.  
In the present review application, the petitioner sought for 
review of the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below, 

<<PAGE 15>>
15 
 
mainly on 3(three) grounds, first one, both the Court’s below 
wrongly taken into consideration the “e¡ ch£e¡j¡” deed dated 
02.04.1965, allegedly executed by the plaintiffs and their mother 
(proforma defendant No.5), through which no title was conferred 
upon the defendants, despite both the Courts below considered the 
side document (fËcnÑe£-P) and the next ground of review was that 
the plaintiffs challenged the deeds (two deeds) allegedly executed 
and registered in the year, 1971, during the ‘disturbed period’, 
through which the defendants claimed the title subsequently, in 
spite of that both the Courts below believed the aforesaid two 
documents (fËcnÑe£-O-1 Hhw O-2) and dismissed the suit as well as 
the appeal and the third one, (which was not taken in the review 
application or argued before the Court of appeal below, but taken 
before this Court in revisional stage) during subsisting of the 
mortgage period the President’s Order No.88 of 1972 has come 
into force, providing the provision that notwithstanding anything 
contained in any mortgage deed or any other sale deed with an 
agreement to reconvey, where the transferor receives from the 
transferee any consideration and whereby the transferee acquires 
right to possess and enjoyment the usufruct of the property, the 

<<PAGE 16>>
16 
 
said transfer shall deem to be a complete usufuuctuary mortgage 
for a period not exceeding 7(seven) years and learned Judge of the 
appellate Court below failed to consider the aforesaid provision.  
From the judgment of the appellate Court below as well as 
the trial Court, it appears that the learned Judges have taken into 
consideration and believed the “e¡ c¡h£e¡j¡” deed of the year 1965 
in deciding the case. Learned Advocate for the petitioner 
contended that ‘e¡ c¡h£e¡j¡’ deed independently cannot confer any 
title upon any person. This Court is in agreement with the 
aforesaid submission, although ‘e¡ c¡h£e¡j¡’ deed does not confer 
any title, but it can be used as co-lateral or associate evidence 
together with the other registered instrument. In the case in hand, 
the principal document, i.e. the mortgage deed in question 
executed in the year 1958 and considering the ‘e¡ c¡h£e¡j¡’ deed 
together with the mortgage deed of the year 1958 is not an error 
on the face of record; although, there is scope of an arguable case, 
whether believing and considering that document together with 
the mortgage deed is legally sound or not, but that argument is to 

<<PAGE 17>>
17 
 
be considered in a different jurisdiction not in review under order 
XLVII of the Civil Code. 
The question of believing or disbelieving the deeds 
executed in the year 1971, during the liberation war cannot be a 
ground of review, because it is a mere question of fact depends 
upon availability of evidences within the record for satisfaction of 
the Courts below, and the said question of believing cannot be 
termed as an apparent error on the face of the record. For sake of 
argument, if the said consideration is not even a sound one or 
seems to be erroneous, such a criticism cannot be looked into on a 
review application filed under Order XLVII, rule 1 within it’s 
limited scope. So far the third ground is concerned, taken by the 
petitioner before the High Court Division in the instant revision, it 
is true section 95A of the SAT Act provides that notwithstanding 
anything contained in any document relating to mortgage or sale 
with a further condition of reconvey, shall be deemed to be a 
complete usufructuary mortgage for a period not exceeding 
7(seven) years. Meaning thereby, from the deed in question if the 
said provision is attracted in any case, then after expiry of 

<<PAGE 18>>
18 
 
7(seven) years the executed mortgage shall be ended treating it as 
an usufructuary mortgage and the property is liable to be 
reconveyed and released in favour of the mortgagor. In the said 
provision it is also stipulated that the provision of section 95 of the 
SAT Act shall apply to such transfer, in particular, sub-section (4) 
and (5) shall apply to such transaction whether made before or 
after the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and 
Tenancy Order (P.O.No.88 of 1972). Meaning thereby, the 
mortgagor after expiry of 7(seven) years from the date of 
execution of the mortgage deed shall be entitled to invoke 
jurisdiction provided under section 95 sub-section (4) and (5) of 
the SAT Act before the Sub-divisional Magistrate or to any officer 
empowered by the Government for that purpose of restoration of 
the land or possession in favour of the mortgagor. Admittedly, the 
petitioner opted to file the redemption suit without invoking the 
jurisdiction under section 95 of the SAT Act, thus, the onus 
heavily lies upon the plaintiff to prove that the transaction or 
mortgage was alive on the date of promulgation of the President’s 
Order No.88 of 1972 and the transaction was not a past and closed 
one, i.e. till 03.08.1972 the status of the mortgaged property 

<<PAGE 19>>
19 
 
having not been changed and it was legally redeemable without 
any change. In the judgment of the appellate Court below, learned 
Judge found that the mortgage has been ended in the year, 1971 by 
2(two) registered saf kabala deeds and the Judge also relied upon a 
deed of ‘e¡ c¡h£e¡j¡ fœ’ executed in the year, 1965. Believing or 
disbelieving any documents or evidences cannot be a ground of 
review treating such judicial findings of fact as an apparent error 
on the face of the record.  
For challenging the aforesaid consideration or aforesaid 
documents, the plaintiffs-petitioners ought to have invoked the 
other jurisdiction available under the Code of Civil Procedure; but 
in an application for review there is hardly any scope to consider 
those grounds. And if the mortgage is ended or the transaction is 
closed before the promulgation of the President’s Order No.88 of 
1972, then section 95A of the SAT Act has no application, 
because, there is nothing alive to restore or redeem. Moreover, 
without taking any such ground or argument before the Court 
concerned against whose judgment the review is sought for, there 
is hardly any scope to consider such new ground in revision 

<<PAGE 20>>
20 
 
before the High Court Division against the rejection of review 
application. 
The cited judgments are of no assistance to improve the 
petitioners’ case; because, in all of those cases the party concerned 
invoked the jurisdiction of sections 95(4) and (5) of the SAT Act, 
applying before the Sub-divisional Magistrate, the simple 
questions were there to restore the land or it’s possession.  
In the premise above, this Court finds no illegally in 
rejecting the review application by the Court of appeal below 
against the judgment and decree dated 11.03.2013 passed in Other 
Class Appeal No. 80 of 2006.  
Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to 
cost.  
  Send down the Lower Courts’ Record. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Obaidul Hasan/B.O.
input_summary: The plaintiffs sued for redemption of a mortgage, recovery of possession and a declaration that the record of rights and the defendants' deeds were void, and lost in the trial court and in the first appeal. They then applied for review of the appellate judgment, raising among other matters the discovery of fresh material and errors said to be apparent on the face of the record. The review application was turned down, the court holding that no such error or sufficient cause had been shown. The plaintiffs carried that order here, pressing a fresh reading of the mortgage documents and of the tenancy statute.
explanation: The court explained that the tenancy statute allows a mortgagor to seek restoration of redeemed land before the revenue authorities after the prescribed period, and that the petitioner, having chosen to sue for redemption instead, had to show the mortgage was still alive when the relevant presidential order was promulgated. The appellate court had found, on two registered deeds and an earlier instrument, that the mortgage had ended years before that date. The court held that weighing evidence or documents is not a ground for review, that such complaints must be raised in appeal, and that fresh points not urged below could not be entertained in revision against the review order.

District: Jessore 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BANGLADESH 
HIGH COURT DIVISION 
(CIVIL REVISIONAL JURISDICTION) 
 
    Present 
 
 
Mr. Justice Sardar Md. Rashed Jahangir 
 
Civil Revision No. 1867 of 2024 
In the matter of : 
Md. Shariful Islam  
                           
 
 
… Petitioner 
 
 
-Versus- 
 
Most. Farhana Akter 
 
       
 
 
…Opposite-party 
 
Mr. Md. Al-Hasan, Advocate 
…for the petitioner 
 
Mr. Amio Chakrabarti, Advocate 
 
 
 
…For the opposite-party 
 
         
Heard on: 24.10.2024 
       
 
Judgment on: 07.11.2024 
 
Rule was issued on an application under section 115(1) of 
the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the opposite-party to 
show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 21.06.2023 
passed by the District Judge, Jessore in Family Appeal No. 17 of 
2023 dismissing the appeal affirming the judgment and order 
dated 04.06.2023 passed by the Family Court and Assistant 
Judge, Jhikargacha, Jessore in Family Suit No. 142 of 2022 
rejecting the application for stay of further proceedings of 

<<PAGE 2>>
2 
 
Family Suit No. 142 of 2022, pending hearing of the C. R. Case 
No. 260 of 2022 of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka 
and Other Class Suit No. 1669 of 2022 should not be set aside 
and/or such other or further order or orders as to this Court may 
seem fit and proper. 
The present opposite party as plaintiff filed Family Suit 
No. 142 of 2022 before the Family Court, Jessore sought for a 
decree for dower and monthly maintenance. The defendant-
petitioner appeared before the Court and filed written statement 
denying all the averments of the plaint. On 04.06.2023 the 
defendant filed an application before the family Court, Jessore 
sought for staying of all further proceedings of Family Suit No. 
142 of 2022 during pendency of the C. R. Case No. 260 of 2022 
of the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and Other 
Class Suit No. 1669 of 2022 pending before the Senior Assistant 
Judge, Second Court, Dhaka. Learned Judge of the family Court 
after hearing the application by his order dated 04.06.0203 
rejected the same. 
Having been aggrieved by the order dated 04.06.2023 
passed by the Family Court, Jessore, the defendant filed Family 
Appeal No. 17 of 2023 before the District Judge, Jessore and 
learned District Judge after hearing by his judgment and order 

<<PAGE 3>>
3 
 
dated 21.06.2023 rejected the appeal summarily and thereby 
affirmed the order dated 04.06.2024 passed by the Family Court, 
Jessore. 
On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid 
order of learned District Judge, the defendant filed this revisional 
application and obtained the Rule together with an order of stay. 
Mr. Md. Al-Hasan, learned Advocate for the petitioner 
submits that the appellate Court below failed to consider that the 
plaintiff created a forged and fake kabinnama inserting a fake 
amount of Tk.20,00,000/- (twenty lac) as dower in collusion with 
some others, behind the back of the defendant and as such the 
defendant filed a complaint petition being C.R. No. 260 of 22 
under section 406/423/465/468/471 of the Penal Code, 1860 now 
pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. He 
further submits that the defendant also filed a suit before the 
Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka challenging the 
legality and authenticity of the kabinnama in question, created by 
the plaintiff for the purpose of family suit and both the cases i.e. 
civil case and criminal case are pending before the Senior 
Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka and before the Chief 
Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and if the family suit is disposed 
of before adjudication of the aforesaid 2(two) cases, then the 

<<PAGE 4>>
4 
 
defendant-petitioner shall be highly prejudiced and as such he 
prayed for making the Rule absolute and thereby allowing the 
application for stay of all further proceedings of the Family Suit 
No. 142 of 2022. 
On the other hand, Mr. Amio Chakrabarti, learned 
Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that 
the hearing and disposal of the suit pending before the family 
Court is independent and there is no nexus with the aforesaid 
2(two) cases and the claim of the defendant as to the forgery and 
forced kabinnama is very much can be ascertained and decided 
independently in the family suit and thus, both the Courts below 
justly and legal rejected the application for stay and in view of 
the above, he prayed for discharging the Rule. 
It appears that the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff on 
13.10.2020 filed Family Suit No. 190 of 2020 before the Family 
Court and Assistant Judge, Jhikargacha, Jessore, which was 
renumbered as Family Suit No. 142 of 2022 with the prayer for a 
direction upon the defendant to pay the plaintiff’s dower and 
monthly maintenance at the rate of Tk.10,000/- (Ten thousand) 
from 23.08.2019 to 23.09.2020 contending, inter-alia, that the 
plaintiff and defendant got marriage as per Muslim Shariah and 
existing law of the country on 19.05.2017 fixing dower of 

<<PAGE 5>>
5 
 
Tk.20,00,000/-(twenty lac), out of which Tk.2,20,000/- (two lac 
twenty thousand) was paid as ushal. The marriage was 
solemnized and registered on the same day. Later on the 
defendant demanding dower of Tk.7,00,000/-(seven lac) and 
started torture upon the plaintiff and as a result, the plaintiffs 
were compelled to stay at the paternal house of the plaintiff No. 
1. The defendant denied to provide maintenance of the plaintiffs 
and as such they were constrained to file the suit. 
The defendant contested the suit by filing written 
statement contending, inter-alia, that on 19.05.2017 as per 
Muslim Shariah and existing law of the country the defendant 
got marriage the plaintiff fixing dower of Tk.2,00,000/- at the 
presence of plaintiffs in-mates. The marriage took place at Sanzi 
Thai and Chinese Restaurant, Badda, Dhaka. It is also stated that 
at the time of marriage no one from the defendant’s family was 
present in the ceremony. Taking the advantage of aforesaid 
circumstances the plaintiff forged the kabinnama by inserting the  
amount of Tk.20,00,000/-(twenty lac) in place of Tk.2,00,000/- 
(two lac). The defendant already paid Tk.2,20,000/- (two lac 
twenty thousand) to the plaintiff No. 1. Thus, the plaintiff No. 1 
is not entitled to get any more dower from the defendant. 

<<PAGE 6>>
6 
 
During pendency of the suit the defendant filed an 
application before the family Court for examine the handwriting 
of the kabinnama by handwriting expert and while the said 
application was pending, on 04.06.2023, the defendant filed an 
application praying for stay of all further proceedings of Family 
Suit No. 142 of 2022 contending, inter-alia that the defendant 
has already filed a criminal case against the plaintiff No. 1 and 
others with the allegation of forgery which is pending before the 
Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and also filed a civil suit 
before the Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka 
challenging  the legally and authenticity of the forged 
kabinnama, using by the plaintiff for the purpose of the family 
suit. Learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 04.06.2023 
rejected the application for stay. Challenging the aforesaid order 
of the Family Court, the defendant preferred Family Appeal No. 
17 of 2023 before the District Judge, Jessore and learned District 
Judge by his order dated 21.06.2023 rejected the appeal 
summarily. 
From the record, it appears that the present suit is a family 
suit, through which the plaintiff claimed dower and maintenance 
and the defendant made appearance in the suit and claimed that 
the submitted kabinnama is a forged one. To substantiate his 
claim also filed an application for examining the handwriting of 

<<PAGE 7>>
7 
 
the kabinnama by a handwriting expert. The said application is 
also pending before Family Court. Although, the defendant 
claimed that he filed a civil suit wherein the kabinnama in 
question has been challenged, but this Court is of the opinion that 
the Family Court is quite competent to adjudge and ascertain the 
legality or authenticity of the kabinnama or fixation of dower by 
taking proper evidences or even taking the assistance of 
specialized person, such a handwriting expert; thus, I am of the 
view that both the Courts below did not commit any illegality in 
rejecting the application for stay. Accordingly, I do not find any 
merit in the Rule. 
However, since the defendant specially challenged the 
authenticity and legality of the kabinnama and claimed insertion 
of a fake amount of dower in the said kabinnama and for the said 
purpose he has filed an application for examining the 
handwriting or etc. by a handwriting expert; thus, the Family 
Court is hereby directed to dispose of the said application and 
send the kabinnama or related documents for examining through 
the handwriting expert if so necessary. It has been also claimed 
by the defendant that the plaintiff’s earlier marriage through 
kabinnama was solemnized fixing the dower money at 
Tk.50,000/- (the present marriage is the second marriage of the 
plaintiff), the kabinnama of her (plaintiff) brother was registered 

<<PAGE 8>>
8 
 
fixing the dower money at Tk.70,000/- and the defendant is a 
third class employee, thus, it is argued that it is quite absurd to 
fix the dower at Tk.20,00,000/-. On the other hand, it is the 
contention of the defendant that the dower was fixed at 
Tk.2,00,000/-  (two lac) at the time of present marriage. 
In view of the above, the Family Court is further directed 
to provide the defendant adequate opportunity to adduce 
evidences to substantiate his claim. 
With the above direction and observation, the Rule is 
discharged without any order as to cost.  
The order of stay granted at the time of issuance of the 
Rule is hereby recalled. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once. 
 
Obaidul Hasan/B.O.
input_summary: The wife sued her husband in the family court for dower and monthly maintenance, relying on a registered marriage document fixing the dower at a substantial sum of which only a part had been paid, and pleading ill-treatment and neglect. The husband asserted that the document was a forgery, that a far smaller dower had been agreed and paid, and asked the family court to stay the suit until a criminal case and a civil suit he had brought against the wife, both challenging the document, were decided. The family court declined to stay and the appeal from that order was turned down summarily.
explanation: The court found that the family court is competent to decide questions about the authenticity of a marriage document and the quantum of dower on the evidence before it, and may even avail itself of expert assistance, so there was no need to await the outcome of the parallel proceedings. It noted that the husband had already applied for examination of the handwriting on the document and that the application was pending. Upholding the refusal to stay, the court nonetheless directed the family court to dispose of the handwriting application, to send the document for expert examination if required, and to give the husband a full opportunity to lead evidence on his claim of forgery.

defendant-respondent before the Judge of the Civil Court, it

filed

order has been reversed against which the defendant-petitioner

On the other hand, Mr. Tapas Kumar Biswas, learned 
Advocate for the opposite-party submits that learned District 
Judge in his judgment found that the plaintiff in his plaint

entered illegally into the plaintiff’s property in their absence 
and in the year 1991 in a ‘Shalis’ the Headman of the mouza 
directed the defendant to vacant plaintiff’s property, but the 
defendant did not pay any heed to the said direction and thus, 
the plaintiff constrained to file the suit. He next submits that 
learned Judge of the Civil Court solely relaying upon an 
inspection report dated 23.05.2002 submitted by the Additional 
Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Khagrachari Hill District 
dismissed the suit, although the plaintiff filed a written 
objection against the report, despite of the Civil Court Judge 
without allowing the plaintiff to examine his witness or to

adduce any document or giving any opportunity to cross-

Heard learned Advocates of both the parties, on perusal

for the opposite party and from the record it appears that the 
suit was dismissed by the Civil Judge on a preliminary point 
without giving any opportunity to the plaintiff to substantiate 
his objection against the report dated 23.05.2002 or to adduce

be prejudiced in any manner, if the suit is sent back on remand 

<<PAGE 6>>
6 
 
for fresh trial, because the defendant will have ample 
opportunity to defend himself. 
In the premise above, I do not find any merit in the Rule. 
Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as 
to cost. 
The learned Judge of the Civil Court of Khagrachari Hill 
District is hereby directed to hear and dispose of the Civil Suit 
No. 36 of 2000 within 6(six) months after notifying both the 
parties and allowing them to take legal steps as per the

appellate Court below dated 18.11.2020 and learned Judge of 
the Civil Court is also directed to dispose of the suit positively

input_summary: The plaintiff sued in the civil court of a hill district for declaration of title and recovery of possession, pleading that the defendant had entered his land unlawfully while he was away and had ignored a direction of the local headman to vacate. The civil judge threw the suit out at a preliminary stage, relying solely on an inspection report of the revenue officer which stated that the land claimed by the plaintiff and the land held by the defendant were not the same, although the plaintiff had filed a written objection to that report. The district judge, in appeal, remanded the suit for a fresh trial with evidence. The defendant carried that remand here.
explanation: The court found that the suit had been decided on a preliminary point without any opportunity being given to the plaintiff to substantiate his objection to the inspection report, to examine his witnesses, to produce documents or to cross-examine the revenue officer, and that the written statement of the defendant nowhere claimed that he held government land under a khas record. It observed that the defendant would suffer no prejudice by a fresh trial, in which he would be free to defend himself fully. No merit being found in the rule, it was turned down, with a direction to the trial court to hear and dispose of the suit on evidence within a fixed period.
